FinanceTab.title: AI build out: AI gold rush draws crypto firms away from Bitcoin
FinanceTab.text:
Companies that once filled warehouses with computers to earn Bitcoin - a process known as mining - are now using that computing power for AI.

Bitcoin mining companies invested large sums on giant banks of powerful computers as the price of Bitcoin rocketed in recent years.

But those mining companies have faced falling rewards since the value of the cryptocurrency has slumped from its peak in October 2025.

Now many are pivoting to AI and signing deals with companies such as Anthropic - who are spending billions of dollars on the infrastructure needed to keep up in the AI race.

Like AI systems, Bitcoin relies on vast networks of powerful computers housed in data centres.

Because Bitcoin operates without a central authority, these computers verify transactions and are rewarded with newly-created digital coins.

But the rewards have reduced and the value of coins has dropped since last year.

One bitcoin was worth about $124,000 (£91,000) at its peak in October 2025, but has since fallen sharply.

More recently, it has rallied to around $80,000 - meaning it is up almost 30% so far in August.

But, for companies that have already made the change, even that may not be enough to get them to return to the crypto industry, because the switch of use - once made - is expensive to undo.

Industry analysts say Bitcoin mining companies have been pivoting to AI because they have years of experience in finding cheap electricity and efficiently running large data centres.

TerraWulf, Ionic Digital, Core Scientific, Iris Energy, Bitdeer, Riot Platforms and Hut 8 are just some of the companies increasingly diverting investment and infrastructure from bitcoin mining towards AI.

Riot Platforms signed a $9bn, 20-year compute deal with Anthropic earlier this month.

Company names and websites are changing to reflect the shift too.

Applied Blockchain has become Applied Digital.

TerraWulf's website once described the firm as an "infrastructure-focused bitcoin mining company".

It now says it focuses on "next-generation AI and high-performance computing".

Enegix, which opened a huge Bitcoin mining site in Kazakhstan to great fanfare in 2020, is now pivoting too.

"Today, we are moving confidently towards artificial intelligence and planning the gradual alignment of our energy and infrastructure capabilities, both in Kazakhstan and elsewhere, towards the development of AI infrastructure," said the company's chief executive Yerbolsyn Sarsenov.

Enegix says it is in active discussions with AI and HPC (high-performance computing) companies and planning to transform a "significant" portion of the business to AI.

But refitting crypto mines for AI is expensive and in some cases the companies have had to sell some of their Bitcoin holdings to fund the switch.

FinanceTab.title: Iran says it is 'fully prepared' to counter widened US economic sanctions
FinanceTab.text:
Iran has said it is confident it can counter widened US sanctions after Washington announced what it described as an "economic D-Day" against the country to try to isolate it from the global economy.

Iranian Economy Minister Ali Madanizadeh said Tehran was "fully prepared" for the sanctions, which he said would lead to "another defeat" for the US.

Announcing a raft of new measures, US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said any nation financially partnering with Iran would be isolated, and that banks and businesses dealing with Iran would share its isolation if they refused to cut ties.

The moves follow U-turns and extended deadlines from the White House in its efforts to end the conflict.

Bessent described the measures as "the single greatest financial offensive ever" against Iran, which would "tighten the noose and block every potential source of revenue".

Some economists have questioned whether the latest sanctions will be effective, as this depends on the reaction from Iran's trading partners.

These include China, the biggest buyer of Iranian oil, which has ignored previous US sanctions and continued to do business with Tehran.

Last week, another of Iran's trade partners, the United Arab Emirates, said it was halting all financial transactions with the country.

But hours after the US announcement, Iran said it was confident it would continue to trade with other nations.

Madanizadeh said neither China nor Russia had accepted the US measures, and predicted other countries would resist them.

"The government is and was ready and has a two-year plan to manage these events," he told state television, adding Tehran had been "waiting for these plans for a long time".

"We also have our own tools and know how to play the game," he said.

Responding to the US announcement, China said it was firmly opposed to what it called "illegal unilateral sanctions".

Foreign ministry spokesman Lin Jiang said economic pressure tactics would not help resolve problems, and Beijing would safeguard its own interests.

The war has led to hikes in global oil prices, and in response to the latest threat Iran warned it would shut down all oil exports from the region if the war continued.

The Iranian regime has also issued a fresh warning to ships not to pass through the Strait of Hormuz without permission, according to Reuters.

One fifth of the world's oil and gas usually passes through the strait - a narrow waterway south of Iran. But the flow has been effectively blocked by the country since the conflict began at the end of February, leading to higher oil prices globally.

At a press conference earlier on Monday outlining what has been called "Operation Economic Outcast", Bessent said the US was launching an "economic onslaught against Iran's financial connections around the globe".

"Iran now faces a very clear choice with only two paths before them: complete global isolation... or a path back to normalcy with an opportunity to rejoin the global economy," he said.

The treasury secretary claimed America was "no longer managing the Iranian threat, we are ending it".

Bessent said the Treasury had mapped networks, facilitators and financial channels used by Iran to evade sanctions to trade oil.

The department said it had issued determinations against five sectors: digital assets, technology, gold, aviation and shipping. The Treasury has also imposed sanctions on almost 60 entities, individuals and vessels.

In a warning to governments and entities assisting or trading with Iran, he said they could not "claim they are blind to enabling this activity".

He declined to highlight specific countries, but said Trump would be phoning world leaders "with specific requests to cease their interactions with the regime".

While he said it was important to give people time to understand the new sanctions, he added: "They should know that we will move very quickly and that we are serious."

David Oxley, chief climate and commodities economist at Capital Economics, cast doubt on the effectiveness of the sanctions announcement.

"With the renewed US naval blockade already strangling Iran's oil exports, the direct impact of 'economic D-Day' on Iran's energy revenues will be somewhat of a damp squib," he said.

"We suspect that the new package will have only a limited direct impact on Iranian energy flows in the short term."

He said that was partly due to the fact roughly 90% of Iran's oil goes to China, a country "which has not recognised US sanctions in the past and is unlikely to be cowed this time either".

"Generally, the Chinese are against unilateral sanctions," said Ali Vaez, deputy director of the Middle East and North Africa Program at the International Crisis Group.

"They would comply with multilateral or international sanctions, but unilateral sanctions just imposed by the US - they have always seen that as illegitimate," he told BBC Radio 4's Today programme.

And although Iran's neighbours like Pakistan, Turkey and Iraq want to maintain good relationships with the US, they "can't really afford to cut off ties with Iran", Vaez added.

He said putting economic pressure on Tehran "doesn't work" because the Iranian regime is willing to "absorb any pain" and pass that onto its people.

Over the course of the conflict so far, previous threats have included Trump saying in April that "a whole civilisation will die tonight" unless Iran agreed a deal to end the war and unblock the Strait of Hormuz.

The US eventually climbed down from that position after mediator Pakistan intervened and called for more diplomacy.

The economic impact of the Iran war is being felt in the US and across the world. Higher oil prices have fuelled concerns over the cost of living, with petrol and diesel prices much higher than they were a year ago.

In the US, gasoline prices have surpassed $4 a gallon and affordability is among the top concerns of American voters ahead of the mid-term elections in November.

On Monday, a barrel of Brent crude, the global benchmark for oil prices, was $92.

Last week, Bessent announced the US government would intervene in the bond markets and buy back more government debt in a bid to boost demand for bonds and lower borrowing rates.

But the impact of the announcement was short-lived, with long-term borrowing costs bouncing back up a day later.

FinanceTab.title: Who does Iran trade with and what could Trump's 'economic D-Day' mean?
FinanceTab.text:
The US has said "the single greatest financial offensive ever" will help it and Israel end their ongoing war with Iran.

However, Iran is no stranger to these tactics.

The regime has faced near continuous US sanctions since the Islamic Revolution of 1979. In that time, it has developed deep trade ties with several countries which either have a history of ignoring US economic pressure themselves or cannot afford to stop trading with Iran.

As a result, Iran says it is "fully prepared" for the new US sanctions and many economists argue the impact of Washington's latest move will be limited.

So, who does Iran trade with? And could what the US has called an "economic D-Day" have any real impact on Iran?

China is the biggest buyer of Iranian goods, making up 26.9% of its exports in 2025, according data from the International Trade Centre (ITC), a subsidiary of the United Nations and the World Trade Organisation.

There a few caveats to ITC's data, which covers a period before the US-Israel war with Iran began.

First, several economists believe that even before the conflict started, a lot of Iranian oil sales, particularly to China, were underreported for political reasons.

Second, the ITC tallies Iran's exports using mostly the import numbers reported by its trading partners - owing to the difficulty in getting up to date export data from Iran.

Third, import data for some of Iran's trading partners, such as Iraq, is incomplete.

Despite this, Iranian trade's importance to China is clear from its response to the US announcement of "economic D-Day".

It said that it was firmly opposed to what it called "illegal unilateral sanctions", that economic pressure tactics would not help resolve problems and that Beijing would safeguard its own interests.

Turkey is another large trading partner of Iran, according to ITC data, but it has a much friendlier relationship with the US than China.

This puts it in a challenging position. The US has threatened to punish those who continue to trade with Iran as part of its economic pressure tactics.

However, economists point out that Turkey cannot stop trading with it without significant damage to its economy, which is already struggling with inflation running at 31.8%, according to official data, external.

In short, as the only Nato member to share a border with Iran, Turkey has to balance its relationship with military allies and maintaining a relationship with its close economic neighbour.

Like Turkey, Pakistan borders Iran and is one of its biggest export partners, according to ITC data, while also being keen to maintain a good relationship with the US.

But unlike Turkey, Pakistan's top export partner is instead the US, meaning it has more to lose from any economic punishment imposed by Washington.

It is also a key mediator in peace talks between the US and Iran, meaning a breakdown in its relationship with either country could make finding a solution to the conflict even more challenging.

The other complicating factor is that not all of Pakistan's trade with Iran is within the Pakistan government's control.

The BBC has seen evidence that oil is being smuggled across the border from Iran to Pakistan en masse by bikers, some as young as 15.

This was the case before the Iran war began, but data suggests the practice has picked up since.

And though the US and Pakistan's oil firms have pressured Pakistan's government to clamp down on the practice, it has struggled to police remote parts of the 900km border.

The BBC has previously asked the Iranian government to comment on the allegation that it is involved in the fuel smuggling. It did not respond.

Armenia is another major trading partner of Iran, according to the ITC data.

Where it differs the most from others is that its top export partner is Russia, which accounts for 34.9% of all goods sold by Armenia in 2025.

This is despite the fact that Russia has faced sanctions from the US and its allies since its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.

This suggests Armenia may be willing to continue trading with Iran despite mounting US pressure.

US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said the sanctions against Iran will "tighten the noose and block every potential source of revenue".

Yet, many experts disagree. Advisory firm Oxford Economics said the direct impact on Iran's revenues would be "somewhat of a damp squib".

Ali Vaez, deputy director at the International Crisis Group, said: "Anything that moves in Iran has already been sanctioned by multiple layers of sanctions, in fact.

"So the question now is one of enforcement. Does the United States have what it takes to impose fines and levies on countries that continue to trade with Iran?"

He noted how the US started an economic war with China, Iran's biggest trading partner, last year but "backed out of it".

Former senior advisor at the state department Aya Ibrahim said the US's overreliance on them "incentivises countries to find ways around that system".

She also raised concerns that the sanctions may have the biggest affect on people, rather than economies, as they "deny people necessities to stay alive".

Meanwhile, global markets have had a muted response to the announcement.

Global oil prices fell following the announcement, but are still far higher than pre-war levels.

Stock traders were even less moved by the news, with the major indexes of the biggest companies listed in the US, Europe, and Asia barely shifting.

The US will has a way to go before it convinces economists, investors, and the nations trading with Iran that its sanctions threat is to be taken seriously.

Additional reporting by Miguel Roca-Terry

FinanceTab.title: Andy Burnham refuses to rule out tax rises in autumn Budget
FinanceTab.text:
Andy Burnham has refused to rule out tax rises in the upcoming autumn Budget, saying he "won't be unrealistic" about the "challenging" state of public finances.

The prime minister said he would take a "careful approach" to the economy, and defended his previously announced cost of living pledges as funded spending commitments.

Burnham became prime minister in July promising to give people breathing space and help with the cost of living, but questions remain over how major policies such as social care reforms will be funded.

Experts have previously warned that he and Chancellor John Healey will have little financial room to manoeuvre in their first Budget on 28 October.

Speaking during his first visit to Ukraine, Burnham said the policies announced so far including capping bus fares at £2 and cutting VAT on household electricity bills were "the first steps that I've felt able to make", and were doable because he was able to reprioritise funding from elsewhere.

"I took the decision early on that digital ID wasn't the top priority for now. And so we've reprioritised funding to other priorities," he said in an interview with ITV.

Asked if the public needed to accept some of the new policies would have to be paid for in tax rises, Burnham said they wouldn't necessarily have to accept that.

Pushed on whether he would need to raise taxes to cover spending gaps, he said: "I will always take a careful approach to things. I ran Greater Manchester for 10 years and we ran a very tight ship with rock solid finances.

"Nothing will change as I come into this role as prime minister. I won't take risks with people's jobs or their livelihoods or their family finances.

"I will try to help them in whatever way I can, I have already done some things that will help them."

Burnham previously told the BBC he accepts his earlier announcements aimed at tackling the cost of living are not enough on their own and hinted at further support.

Speaking during his first official overseas visit on Monday, he said while he would do what he could, "I won't be unrealistic and people really need to understand that.

"We are in a challenging position, whatever I do will be carefully thought through, it will be funded and there will be more to come as we go into the autumn."

Last week official figures showed the the government borrowed more than expected in July, despite a record month for income tax receipts.

Inflation also reached a four-month high of 2.9% in July and is expected to rise further due to the ongoing impact of the Iran war, which has hit energy prices and fuel costs.

Experts have warned Burnham and Healey that they need to either raise taxes or cut spending elsewhere as pressure on the public finances has left no room for extra borrowing.

Both the prime minister and chancellor have vowed to stick to the fiscal rules set by former chancellor Rachel Reeves.

The rules are designed to ensure day-to-day spending is funded through tax revenue by the end of the Parliament, and to reduce debt as a proportion of GDP.

Rain Newton-Smith, chief executive of the Confederation of British Industry, said business owners wanted to create opportunities for young people but "the cost of employing people has gone up so much".

"The business leaders I speak to say that the cost of doing business has gone up so much that it's holding them back from creating opportunities," she told the Today programme.

She said targeted support for businesses would create "more growth and more opportunities that saves money for the government and ultimately leads to higher tax receipts".

FinanceTab.title: 81,000 warning letters sent to crypto holders in HMRC tax crackdown
FinanceTab.text:
HM Revenue and Customs (HMRC) sent more than 81,000 letters warning cryptocurrency holders they may owe capital gains tax in the past year.

A Freedom of Information (FOI) request seen by the BBC showed the number of letters sent by the tax authority had almost tripled since 2024.

Investors could face fines or prosecution if they fail to declare profits they made from selling, even if they exchange one cryptocurrency for another.

New powers due to be given to HMRC next year will make it easier to target wealthy crypto investors, with one analyst saying investigations will be like "shooting fish in a barrel".

"There is the expectation amongst tax authorities that cryptocurrency investment is rife with tax evasion," says Neela Chauhan, partner at UHY Hacker Young - which carried out the FOI.

"A lot of the traders are young, have had little previous exposure to HMRC and often work under the assumption that HMRC has limited visibility over their activities."

In the 2025-26 financial year, HMRC sent 81,172 warning letters, emails and text messages to crypto investors it suspects may have underpaid tax.

The number in 2023-24 was just 27,714.

An HMRC spokesperson said: "We’re committed to helping people pay the right amount of tax, and the vast majority do.

"We regularly send letters to educate, remind or prompt customers to review their tax affairs, including customers who use crypto assets."

FinanceTab.title: Canada announces retaliatory tariffs on wide range of US goods
FinanceTab.text:
Canada has announced it will impose tariffs on a wide range of key American industries including cosmetics, dairy, wood products and outdoor equipment in the coming weeks, as it retaliates roughly “dollar for dollar” against levies imposed by the US.

In a strong Canadian countermove to tariffs levied by Donald Trump, which took effect on Saturday after trade talks collapsed the day before, Canada’s finance and industry ministers on Tuesday called the measure a “focused response” to what they see as unfair trade practices.

The White House claimed it was using section 338 of the Tariff Act of 1930 to protest against “discriminatory” trade policies by Canada, including provincial bans on US alcohol – a ban that was only implemented in protest against tariffs imposed on Canadian goods last year.

The prime minister, Mark Carney, had previously pledged a “dollar-for-dollar” response from his government after roughly 5% of exports to the US were singled out by the White House.

The retaliatory Canadian measures will cover C$27.6bn ($19.9bn) in imports and are meant to target key industries including steel, dairy, appliances, agricultural equipment, pulp and paper.

The list from Ottawa has more than 700 items, ranging from from hockey sticks to ornamental fish and toilet paper to smoked lobster, with most of the tariffs set at 25% or 50%. A small group of items, including air conditioning units and tool parts, will face a lower 15% tariff. The levies will be effective starting 8 September and only apply to goods originating from the US.

In announcing the retaliatory measures, the finance minister, François-Philippe Champagne, said the country was united in its fight against the US, telling attenders that Canada remained “masters of our own home”.

The industry minister, Mélanie Joly, called on businesses and consumers to buy Canadian goods as part of a broader “resistance” movement in the trade war.

“You have power,” she said.

The government also announced more than C$7bn in support for businesses affected by the latest tariffs, adding to more than C$20bn in support announced over the past 18 months.

Canada’s decision to retaliate means both countries have doubled down on a trade war that could cost billions.

Earlier on Tuesday, Trump said he was giving “serious consideration” to changing the name of Lake Ontario to “Lake America” – reminiscent of his decision to rename the Gulf of Mexico to the Gulf of America. Others pointed out that Ontario, Canada’s most populous province, was named after the lake, not the other way around.

Trump’s frustration with Ontario in particular stems from his feud with the province’s premier, Doug Ford, who called the president a “loser” and the “king of bankruptcies” and told the US president to “kiss my ass”. He also threatened to cut electricity and rare earth metal exports to the US.

Trump called Ford a “flunky” of “Governor Carney” and warned “these clowns to ‘fall in line’ or, the consequences for Canada will be far WORSE!”

Trump later alluded to revelations that his trade negotiators had looked to weaken French language rules, saying he would “never interfere” with Canadians speaking French, calling it a “lie … made up by a weak and ineffective Prime Minister in an attempt to gain political support”.

Trump later added: “I love French Canadians!”

SportsTab.title: Ayyoub Bouaddi: Manchester City sign Morocco midfielder from Lille in £86m deal
SportsTab.text:
Manchester City have signed midfielder Ayyoub Bouaddi from Lille in a £85.6m deal to make the Morocco international the Premier League's most expensive teenager.

The 18-year-old joins on a five-year contract, subject to international clearance, with City paying £81.4m upfront plus £4.2m in add-ons.

Enzo Maresca's side moved to sign Bouaddi after selling central midfielders Rodri to Barcelona in a £65m deal and Tijjani Reinders to Al-Qadsiah for £52m.

He impressed at this summer's World Cup - starting five of Morocco's six matches in their run to the quarter-finals - after becoming a key member of Lille's side in Ligue 1.

"This is a very special day for me and my family. Manchester City are, for me, the best club in the world. It's a dream to be here and be able to call myself a City player," said Bouaddi.

"I have spent most of my life working hard to become the best player I can be and reach the top of the game.

"I've watched City for many years, and I love their style of play. City always try and play quality football. And they have shown they are winners - this club feels like it's built to win."

The fee for Bouaddi surpasses the £58.9m paid by Manchester United to sign French defender Leny Yoro, also from Lille, in 2024.

Bouaddi made 96 appearances for Lille after making his debut in 2023, helping them finish third in Ligue 1 last season.

At the age of 16 he became the youngest footballer to ever play for the French side on his senior debut against Faroese club KI in the Europa League, before announcing himself on the world stage by playing a starring role in Lille's Champions League victory over Real Madrid in 2024.

Bouaddi will form part of a revamped midfield, with City already bringing in England midfielder Elliot Anderson from Nottingham Forest for £116m.

Bouaddi functions as a deep-lying conductor and would complement Anderson, who is comfortable as a box-to-box midfielder as well as the number six role he plays for England.

City are also set to make an offer for Chelsea's Argentina midfielder Enzo Fernandez but it remains to be seen whether a deal can be struck with the 25-year-old valued at £120m.

Bouaddi's signing comes after Brazilian winger Savinho, now known as Savio, joined Tottenham in a £75m deal earlier this week.

SportsTab.title: Brydon Carse: Josh Tongue says Joe Root's message to England players has "100%" landed
SportsTab.text:
Fast bowler Josh Tongue said captain Joe Root's message to the England players about their off-field behaviour has "100%" been heeded.

On Tuesday, Root said he was "hacked off" that Brydon Carse had become the latest England player involved in a late-night drinking controversy.

The skipper also revealed he had addressed the squad before they began training in preparation for the second Test against Pakistan at Lord's, beginning on Thursday.

"It was a chat that was needed, a very good chat from Rooty," Tongue told BBC Sport.

"He was very clear on the message of what it is like to be an England cricketer. We're very privileged to put on that England shirt and we want to show kids growing up how good it is to play for England in front of thousands of people."

Carse has been removed from the England squad for the second Test after he was briefly arrested while on a night out in Derby on Saturday.

Footage of the 31-year-old in handcuffs and surrounded by police officers appeared on social media on Sunday.

He was eventually de-arrested, but the England and Wales Cricket Board have referred the matter to the Cricket Regulator, and the Regulator's investigation has resulted in Carse's absence from the squad for Lord's.

It is the latest in a string of controversies involving the England men's team over the past 10 months.

Only last week, before the first Test in his second spell as captain, Root called on his players to be "really good role models and good human beings".

This week, Root made no attempt to hide his frustration at "stupid mistakes".

On what Root said to the players, Tongue revealed: "He was honest with us all in the changing room. He said it straight. As soon as that chat was finished, our focus was fully on these next five days."

Asked if the message had "landed", Nottinghamshire's Tongue replied: "Yeah, 100%. What has happened in the past is the past and we need to try to move on from that."

Tongue is one of the eight England centrally contracted players to have been involved in or present for a late-night drinking incident since last October.

The 28-year-old was with Harry Brook when the England white-ball captain was punched by a nightclub bouncer in Wellington.

The Regulator took no action against Tongue for his part in the controversy, but the paceman admitted he was forced to reflect on his involvement and the fragility of a career as an England cricketer.

"I want to play for England for as long as I can," he said. "I've tried to forget about that as much as I can and focus on the cricket here, now."

Tongue was part of a four-pronged pace attack that led England to an innings victory over Pakistan in the first Test at Headingley.

Victory over the tourists at Lord's would give England their first win in a multi-match series since 2024.

The hosts seem likely to name an unchanged XI, the first time they have gone unchanged between matches since the first and second Tests at home to India last summer.

England are currently under interim head coach Marcus Trescothick, with New Zealander Stephen Fleming due to take charge from the tour of South Africa in December.

In Leeds, Root confirmed he had been in daily contact with Fleming, and Tongue has also heard from the incoming coach.

"He messaged me the day before the Test, touching on The Hundred and congratulating me on that, and saying good luck for the first Test," said Tongue.

"Then he messaged me after the first day as well, which was very nice. Obviously, he wants to have a look at everyone before coming in for the South Africa series. It's nice to know that he's been watching."

SportsTab.title: Man City to bid for Chelsea's £120m-rated Enzo Fernandez
SportsTab.text:
Manchester City are set to make an opening offer for Chelsea midfielder Enzo Fernandez.

The Argentina international has been identified by manager Enzo Maresca as a priority target to bolster City's midfield after a series of high-profile exits.

Chelsea are aware of City's interest and set an unofficial deadline for the deal to be completed earlier this summer at a minimum fee of £120m only for that date to pass.

Nevertheless, City are expected to return with another attempt to sign the 25-year-old before next week's transfer deadline.

Fernandez could become one of the most expensive signings in Premier League history, behind only Liverpool's £125m move for Alexander Isak last summer.

Fernandez maintains a positive relationship with Maresca, who left Chelsea in controversial fashion on New Year's Day and moved to Etihad Stadium in June.

It could potentially be the second time City break their transfer record in the same window having paid £116m to recruit Elliot Anderson from Nottingham Forest.

There have also been four major midfield departures, with Tijjani Reijnders sold to Saudi Arabian club Al-Qadsiah for £52m, while Barcelona have signed Rodri for £65m, Newcastle have agreed a £52m deal to sign Nico Gonzalez and Bernardo Silva departed earlier in the summer before joining Real Madrid.

It has been a turbulent period for Fernandez at Stamford Bridge, during which he and his agent, former Paris St-Germain midfielder Javier Pastore, courted interest from Real Madrid, only for the Spanish club to issue a statement denying any attempt to sign him.

The situation has been ongoing since Chelsea were knocked out of the Champions League by PSG in March, after which Fernandez became increasingly critical of the club.

New Chelsea manager Xabi Alonso spoke in July about a private conversation he had with Fernandez, who signed for £107m from Benfica in 2023, but declined to disclose details of the discussion.

Fernandez came on as a second-half substitute in Monday's 3-2 win over Fulham and was booed by home supporters because of his role in England's World Cup exit.

After briefly celebrating with the away fans and his team-mates after the final whistle, he was the first Chelsea player to head down the tunnel.

SportsTab.title: Raheem Sterling charged with dangerous driving after crash on M3 in Hampshire
SportsTab.text:
Raheem Sterling will appear in court next month to face charges of dangerous driving and possessing nitrous oxide for wrongful inhalation after crashing his car into motorway barriers in May.

The former England winger, who most recently played for Feyenoord in the Dutch Eredivisie, crashed his Lamborghini into barriers on the M3 in Hampshire on the morning of Thursday, 28 May.

The 31-year-old was arrested and then released on bail pending further enquiries.

A Hampshire & Isle of Wight Constabulary spokesman said: "A driver will appear in court next month to face charges following a collision on the M3.

"Raheem Sterling, 31, from Berkshire, has been charged for the following offences: dangerous driving, possession of nitrous oxide for wrongful inhalation, failing to provide a specimen.

"The charges come following a single vehicle collision, involving a Lamborghini, on the M3 southbound, close to the Minley Interchange [Hampshire], on 28 May, 2026.

"No other vehicles were involved and no injuries were reported. Mr Sterling is due to appear at Basingstoke magistrates court on 15 September."

Police suspected Sterling of "driving a vehicle whilst unfit through drugs," but that has not been included in the charges.

In May a source close to Sterling told BBC Sport there was "no proof" of drugs in his system.

The source added the player had faced "an extremely tough couple of years" and had been made to "feel worthless" and "forgotten about".

Sterling has been without a club since leaving Dutch side Feyenoord at the end of last season.

He joined Feyenoord in February on a short-term contract after leaving Chelsea by mutual consent.

Chelsea paid £47.5m to sign Sterling from Manchester City in 2022, where he had won four Premier League titles, five League Cups and one FA Cup in seven years.

In 2024 the former Liverpool winger joined Arsenal on loan, but upon returning to Chelsea in 2025 was exiled from the first-team squad and made to train separately.

Sterling earned 82 England caps between 2012 and 2022, and appeared at three World Cups and two European Championships.

SportsTab.title: Celtic deficiencies laid bare at LASK on another night of Champions League pain
SportsTab.text:
When Callum McGregor eviscerated his own team-mates in the wake of Celtic's stupefying Champions League collapse against LASK, he delivered their one coherent moment of a spineless night.

In branding his fellow players "passive" and "scared" and in then sending a telling shot across their bows - "now we'll see what people are made of" - it is hard to recall him being so full of fury after a European game.

And there are plenty to choose from, plenty of dark nights, plenty of embarrassment, plenty of soul-searching over many years.

For close to a decade he has been Celtic's best player, a near ever-present. That longevity has brought him many trophies, but he's been around for many mortifications, too.

Where losing a 4-0 advantage ranks in the pantheon of Celtic failures is a moot point. What is unarguable is that it was a total capitulation, a feeble collapse in the face of LASK's physicality and desire and belief.

The Celtic captain called his players "scared" when winning 4-0. No media hatchet man could come up with a more damaging word to describe what happened out there.

McGregor has been through the European mill.

He was there last season when Celtic's fecklessness saw them go goalless for 210 minutes against the popgun boys of Kairat Almaty before failing to score from three of their five penalties in the shootout.

He was there for the 7-1 against Borussia Dortmund and the 6-0 against Atletico Madrid.

He's a survivor of the Champions League play-off exit to Midtjylland and the pair of 4-1 losses to Sparta Prague in the Europa League.

He was around for earlier Champions League play-off exits against Ferencvaros, AEK Athens and Cluj.

He's a veteran of the 7-1 loss to PSG and the 7-0 loss to Barcelona. He wears the scars as much as he holds the medals.

It is difficult, though, to recall him being as seething as he was on Tuesday night.

He wasn't ranting - that is not his style. He spoke calmly which lent his words more power.

He was raging in his own way. Raging at another exit, raging that when the chips were down too many of his fellow players panicked and allowed themselves to be overrun, raging at professional pride being trampled underfoot for all to see.

It was McGregor who opened the scoring on the night, a deflected shot and a 4-0 lead on aggregate.

LASK had started well but that goal looked to all the world like a kick to their solar plexus. They had chances in Glasgow and they had chances in the opening minutes in Linz - and they were 4-0 down!

How many punches can one team take before they lose their fight? Many, as it turned out.

Celtic were obliging, of course. Painfully so. We trumpeted their classy goals and their adventurous play a week ago and wrongly assumed that they had gumption to go with it. Big mistake.

When Benjamin Nygren's ridiculously loose pass led directly to LASK's equaliser on the night, the first signs of a wobble were visible.

Thirty two minutes had been played and Celtic did not look wholly comfortable at 4-1 on aggregate. Mad, but true.

When they conceded again three minutes into the second half, there were a few jelly legs on show. Auston Trusty was culpable this time. Brushed off the ball. Swatted and 4-2 now.

Trusty was poor, not the only one, but a point of real weakness that LASK went for.

Ten minutes after the hosts scored their second, they scored their third. Too many parts of the Celtic team were in full fright mode now. The slow death was picking up pace.

Camilo Duran, the hero of the first leg, was reduced to a non-event. Kasper Hogh worked hard but with no impact. Passes went astray. Celtic were directionless. Everything fell apart.

Rabbits in headlights do not tend to look as lost as Celtic did when the pressure really hit.

If McGregor was trying to put out fires in his own team he was failing. He could not cut through the tension.

Martin O'Neill looked on like a man 10 years older than his true age. This was a shocking night for him. One of his worst in football, he said later. He took responsibility, but he cannot be alone in that.

He emptied his bench in a desperate attempt to stem the flow, but his substitutions, five in 12 befuddled minutes, had zero impact.

Celtic did not have a shot on target in the second half of normal time nor in extra-time. They only existed as a man hanging off a cliff edge exists. There was only one way this was going to end.

LASK's fourth goal might have come in the 90th minute but it was deserved.

By that point they'd had 33 shots on Celtic's goal (they finished on 40) to go with the 20 from last week. It was a rout.

Cameron Carter-Vickers was hobbling about on one leg. Hogh much the same. Forward came the waves and Celtic tried to hold them back with a back four of Anthony Ralston, Dane Murray, Trusty and Liam Scales.

The fifth goal was a mercy, and another Celtic player doing the wrong thing at the wrong time in the wrong place. For Nygren and Trusty read Luke McCowan. Hapless and helpless - and out of the Champions League.

The night meandered to its conclusion. LASK missed a penalty for 6-1 before Miguel Freckleton, recently of St Mirren, slalomed his way into the Celtic box and threatened, for a second, to score.

All credit to Freckleton and his new beginning in Austria, but in flashes he was made to look like a serious player in his few minutes on the pitch. When that kind of thing happens it tells a story.

Celtic were beyond disarray by then. Spooked, over-powered, out-fought, out-played. The smooth-running killers of last week in Glasgow was an optical illusion that hid psychological deficiencies.

Nobody could have predicted that they would fall in such a heap at 4-0, but they did.

Celtic, quite obviously, need a back-up left-back to Kieran Tierney and they don't have one.

They absolutely need, and this is no secret, a physical presence in the middle of the pitch, a player of stature in every sense of the word, a guy who would not be bullied as Celtic were bullied in Austria. They don't have one of those either.

They have done good deals but not enough of them. They're in net profit in their transfer business this summer.

The A-word - ambition - is going to get another airing. When you finish a £40m match with a back four of Ralston, Murray, Trusty and Scales then, as a club, you have not done your work properly. Nobody did on the night, on the field and off.

All those other defeats were incredibly costly in a financial but also in a self-worth sense.

They hoped they'd left the Champions League drawing board behind, but they're right back where they were when Kairat and Midtjylland and Ferencvaros and Cluj and AEK were the ones inflicting the pain.

Incredibly, another name has to get added to the list.

SportsTab.title: Cristiano Ronaldo: Ten-man Al-Nassr seal dramatic win after Portugal star subbed off
SportsTab.text:
Cristiano Ronaldo was taken off at half-time with his 10-man Al-Nassr side 2-0 down - before they fought back to seal a dramatic win over Al-Ettifaq.

Defending Saudi Pro League champions Al-Nassr got off to a dreadful start on Tuesday when goalkeeper Bento was sent off after just 12 minutes and they were two goals behind at the break.

Ronaldo, 41, making his first start since the World Cup, left the pitch in frustration at half-time and was then substituted by manager Ange Postecoglou.

But Postecoglou's decisions proved to be vindicated with Al-Nassr launching a second-half comeback.

Sadio Mane and Abdulelah Al Amri scored inside three minutes to draw Al-Nassr level with 13 minutes to go, before former Liverpool forward Mane got the winner in added time.

The win helped Al-Nassr go top of the table after three straight victories this season.

Former Tottenham and Nottingham Forest boss Postegoclou said Ronaldo, who spread his arms in a questioning gesture towards the bench when he was substituted, was taken off as part of a different tactical approach.

"When I made the substitutions, including taking Ronaldo off, I believed the players coming on could make an impact," Postecoglou said.

"I came here to help the players, so as I said, I'm proud of them because every substitute made a positive contribution.

"I'm here to help the team with what I see, and everyone knows that Ronaldo hasn't played in a long time. He performed exceptionally well in the first half, and we opted for a different approach."

Postecoglou took over at Al-Nassr last month after being sacked by Forest last October following just 39 days in charge.

SportsTab.title: US Open 2026: Serena Williams and Carlos Alcaraz return in mixed doubles
SportsTab.text:
Enjoy it - and do what Serena Williams tells you to.

That was how Carlos Alcaraz settled back into competitive action at the US Open, partnering the American great as she returned to her home slam after a four-year absence.

The tournament's revamped mixed doubles format has attracted criticism for favouring the allure of the sport's top singles stars at the expense of established doubles players.

But the crowds turned out and produced a terrific atmosphere for the tournament's headline act, with about 15,000 people packed inside Arthur Ashe Stadium.

All four doubles specialist pairings lost to a team of singles players on Tuesday, while Alcaraz and Williams fell in the quarter-finals.

Seven-time major winner Alcaraz was playing his first competitive match since April after injuring his wrist, while 23-time Grand Slam champion Williams was competing in New York for the first time since she "evolved away" from tennis in 2022.

The pair were greeted by huge cheers and were roared on throughout their opening 5-3 4-1 win against Great Britain's Lloyd Glasspool and New Zealand's Erin Routliffe.

The 44-year-old Williams won the US Open mixed doubles title in its original format alongside Max Mirnyi in 1998 - five years before Alcaraz was born.

Almost 30 years later, Williams still had the competitive desire. She and Alcaraz enjoyed the occasion, playing with smiles on their faces and roaring each other on after winning a point.

Interviewed during a change of ends, Alcaraz said: "I'm playing next to the one and only Serena Williams, so what else can I do? Just enjoy and try to do the things she told me to do."

Their partnership improved rapidly in their first match as they won eight of the final nine games to seal victory.

However, they were denied a place in Wednesday's semi-finals by Italy's world number six Flavio Cobolli and Swiss team-mate Belinda Bencic, who won 5-4 (7-4) 4-1.

While Williams will not contest the singles at the US Open - she has not competed in that format since injuring her knee at Wimbledon - Tuesday's matches provided the returning Alcaraz with valuable court time.

The Spaniard admitted he felt nervous before stepping out on the court - in part due to partnering six-time US Open women's singles champion Williams.

"I think everyone could see I was really nervous, I double-faulted on the first point," Alcaraz said after their opening win.

"I was out for almost five months and I almost forgot how it feels stepping out on the court once again.

"It [took] just a couple of games [to settle] and she made it very easy for me to enjoy it and try to go for it."

For Williams, a return to the Arthur Ashe Stadium was something she did not believe would come around again.

"It's always amazing to be here. I never expected to be back on this court," Williams said.

"It was just a really cool moment. I never thought this would happen."

Sabalenka and Djokovic lasted just 49 minutes, but this was otherwise a day where the singles stars edged out the doubles specialists.

With none of the four doubles pairs making it to the last four, the USTA has the sort of semi-final line up it envisaged when deciding to reinvent the mixed doubles 12 months ago.

Sabalenka and Djokovic turned out to be a very brief experiment. The other marquee pairing of Williams and Alcaraz lasted longer, with Williams in particular catching the eye in their first round win.

But with Alcaraz looking increasingly rusty in the quarter-final, Cobolli and Bencic won convincingly.

The Spaniard was wearing a compression sleeve on his right arm, and the skin fade of earlier in the year has been replaced by a mop of black hair.

This was useful court time for him, but did not really tell us anything about his chances of remaining in New York for the singles final in just under three weeks time.

SportsTab.title: Liverpool's midfield is fragile - but will they act in the transfer window?
SportsTab.text:
A little over four minutes had passed at St James' Park on Sunday and Liverpool had started encouragingly, keeping the ball well and with urgency in their play.

Ryan Gravenberch created space with a brilliant touch to get past Lewis Miley but instead of shooting from the edge of the box or playing Dominik Szoboszlai through, the Netherlands international lost possession.

Just 11 seconds later, Newcastle were ahead through Anthony Elanga after a devastating counter that required one pass after Amar Dedic's initial clearance.

Liverpool simply had no structure when out of possession. It was schoolboy stuff and a nightmare start for Andoni Iraola.

It was a similar story in the second half when Gravenberch was dispossessed after trying a back heel on the edge of the Newcastle box.

This time, Yoane Wissa went on a brilliant run through the centre - evading an array of Liverpool players - and played the ball to Joe Willock, who finished in style.

As Iraola alluded to after, perhaps one of his players should have had the know how to commit a foul in that situation but Liverpool were punished again.

Looking back on both goals, Gravenberch's decision-making should have been better and perhaps the centre-back pairing of Virgil van Dijk and Jeremy Jacquet could have engaged quicker rather than holding off.

But having a defensive midfielder stationed accordingly would, in all likelihood, have nullified the threat.

Liverpool have not had an out-and-out number six since Fabinho, who left in 2023, and as it stands Iraola's preference is a two-man pivot in midfield with Florian Wirtz playing as a number 10.

Both of those two midfielders, Gravenberch and Szoboszlai, were in the Newcastle box when Liverpool lost possession before Elanga's opener.

If Liverpool are to be taken seriously, they simply cannot concede goals like that regularly.

Iraola tends to avoid major debriefs in the dressing room after a game, with his personal preference to speak to the players a day later.

Asked in his post-match news conference about what could be done to prevent the kind of goals his side conceded, the Liverpool head coach suggested that it was not due to the type or identity of midfielders he had selected.

"I think it's just not personnel," said Iraola. "I understand you are telling me basically that Ryan Gravenberch is the six and he is on the edge of the box - but if he shoots and he scores we are saying what a play from Ryan Gravenberch."

It was an interesting point, given that Gravenberch produced the assist for Cody Gakpo's equaliser.

But shortly after Newcastle went 2-1 up, Iraola reacted by bringing on Alexis Mac Allister for Wirtz and Liverpool did seem more stable defensively - even if the Argentina international prefers to play as an eight.

Szoboszlai made zero tackles and won three of his 10 duels (30%) while Gravenberch similarly failed to make a tackle and won four of his 10 duels (40%).

When Mac Allister came on, he made two tackles and won four of his five duels (80%).

"We have to adapt as a team to these situations and we have to know that these situations can happen," added Iraola.

"I think the second goal, we probably did better in terms of having the numbers to defend - we don't make the foul, or go to the first challenge or probably reduce the distance with the ball carrier, so it's an incredible goal.

"Situations [are] just not because one person is playing there, [it] is something that we have to correct between a lot of players."

At full-time, the xG was 1.43 to Newcastle and 2.73 to Liverpool - indicating Newcastle had ruthlessly seized their opportunities against Iraola's side.

On Sky Sports, former Liverpool striker Daniel Sturridge did not hold back in his criticism.

"Liverpool do not have that profile of player right now." said Sturridge. "The team has needed a defensive midfielder for three years. If you analyse the midfield, they are all naturally attacking players."

At Liverpool, the focus in the remaining days of the transfer window is clear. Their stance is unchanged in that the priority remains wide attacking players rather than midfield, even after the exit of Curtis Jones.

As always, if an opportunity presents itself in the market then Liverpool will consider it but Iraola is understood to be satisfied with his depth in midfield - with Wataru Endo, Trey Nyoni and James McConnell as the back-up options.

Liverpool have previously enquired about Adam Wharton but Crystal Palace's stance is that the 22-year-old is not for sale.

Under Jurgen Klopp, Liverpool tried to get Moises Caicedo in 2023 and when Arne Slot arrived in 2024, Liverpool were keen on signing Martin Zubimendi from Real Sociedad.

But that fell through when the now-Arsenal midfielder turned the move down.

Gravenberch had a brilliant season under Slot as Liverpool cruised their way to the Premier League title, perhaps masking the issues temporarily by covering over emerging cracks.

Liverpool's summer window 12 months ago then became about super-charging their attack with Alexander Isak, Florian Wirtz and Hugo Ekitike, rather than reinforcing the middle of the pitch.

Those fault lines are much clearer now and Iraola will know that his midfield must become harder to break down or else his side will keep on conceding.

SportsTab.title: Joao Pedro: Is Brazilian ready to break Chelsea's so-called number nine curse?
SportsTab.text:
Joao Pedro took just 31 seconds to make a statement about how he is handling the so-called curse of the number nine shirt at Chelsea.

The Brazilian deftly lifted his shot over Fulham goalkeeper Bernd Leno to set his side on their way to a dramatic 3-2 win at Craven Cottage in manager Xabi Alonso's first game in charge on Monday.

It was a memorable weekend for Joao Pedro personally, having been handed the coveted number nine shirt and improved financial terms on a new contract that will run until 2034.

It might seem trite, but there is a sizeable group of Chelsea supporters who believe in the so-called curse.

Not since Dutch striker Jimmy Floyd Hasselbaink left the club in 2004 have the club had a prolific striker in the number nine shirt.

Didier Drogba wore number 11 during his successful spell at Stamford Bridge and Diego Costa had the number 19 shirt, but high-profile forwards including Romelu Lukaku, Alvaro Morata, Gonzalo Higuain, Radamel Falcao and Pierre-Emerick Aubameyang struggled while wearing number nine.

All endured difficult and relatively short periods at the club.

The last player to wear the shirt before Joao Pedro was Liam Delap, who is currently in talks with Nottingham Forest about leaving Stamford Bridge after scoring only one Premier League goal last season.

Non-strikers, including midfielder Steve Sidwell and defender Khalid Boulahrouz, also wore the shirt, although some supporters would argue Tammy Abraham performed well as the number nine before his move to Roma.

Asked about the curse after scoring against Fulham, while starring alongside both Cole Palmer and club-record £117m signing Morgan Rogers, Joao Pedro told the Mirror: "I don't believe in that. I don't think numbers can decide this pressure."

Last season, the 24-year-old matched his shirt number by scoring 20 goals in all competitions, becoming the first Chelsea striker since Diego Costa to reach that mark nine years earlier.

It has left the Blues delighted with the £55m deal, plus up to £5m in add-ons, they agreed with Brighton to sign the forward last summer. Those close to Joao Pedro also believe his recent recognition is justified.

In addition, his close-knit entourage have no concerns about his ability to handle the pressure of being Chelsea's leading man, having shared in his remarkable rise to the top.

"If I gave him one thing, it is to fight for what you want all the time," his mother Flavia Junqueira explained to BBC Sport.

Looking at Joao Pedro's story, that is exactly what he has had to do.

His mother, along with his grandmother, have largely brought him up.

Reports from Joao Pedro's early childhood show his father, former Botafogo footballer Jose Joao de Jesus - more commonly known as Chicao - spent around eight years in prison after being charged as an accessory to murder and was rarely around.

Junqueira later separated from him and focused on her son's footballing potential.

"Joao had a dream," she said. "I shared that dream with my son. The dream didn't have a price."

Growing up in Ribeirao Preto, a nine-hour drive inland from Sao Paulo, Joao Pedro was eventually scouted by one of the city's clubs Fluminense, along with a host of other leading Brazilian clubs.

Fluminense were regarded as the best option for the youngster's development, who, like his father, began as a defensive midfielder before progressing further forward.

That choice was, however, fraught with difficulty.

Junqueira left her job, friends and family for Rio, and Joao Pedro "cried a lot" during the journey and in the weeks that followed because of homesickness.

Even in the academy, he was told he "wasn't strong enough" and would not make it. Again, it made him cry.

But his mother, despite her increasingly limited means after leaving her job, hired a personal trainer for her son.

At first, he ate well and trained well only because she told him to. Eventually, however, the penny dropped.

"He was very skinny and there was a significant physical disparity between him and the other athletes in his age group," his long-time personal trainer Rodrigo Goncalves told BBC Sport.

"He never stopped training. Sometimes he went a bit reluctantly, pushed by his mother, but he went.

"Over the years, however, that changed. He began to mature and understand that training wasn't just something his mother required, but rather a tool to improve his performance, develop his body and build the physical balance needed for football."

Joao Pedro became one of the stars of Fluminense's academy and was spotted by Watford's South America scout Rafa Monfort. A phone call from now-Tottenham striker Richarlison, who had made the same move, also proved crucial.

As a child, Joao Pedro was hooked on Premier League football, so the idea of moving to Watford appealed to him. However, it took around eight months to meet the Governing Body Endorsement criteria and secure a UK work permit.

Junqueira believes an overhead kick scored by Joao Pedro, then 17, against Cruzeiro in May 2019 helped convince decision-makers he was an exceptional talent worthy of the move.

When the family arrived in December 2019, Junqueira had not anticipated her bank cards would not work in England. However, then-Watford goalkeeper Heurelho Gomes, also Brazilian, took them under his wing and even bought them Christmas dinner.

A few months later, Covid and lockdown arrived, but Joao Pedro used the unprecedented period to focus on physical training with Goncalves again. He transformed his body by gaining around eight kilograms of body mass and became Premier League-ready.

After that period, he was no longer the little boy who cried, but a fully-fledged top-flight star capable of taking each step and challenge in his stride.

After a deal was agreed with Brighton last summer, Joao Pedro left a training camp in Rio de Janeiro under the guidance of Goncalves to join the Chelsea squad in Miami and immediately take part in the Fifa Club World Cup.

Remarkably, he scored twice in the semi-final against former club Fluminense - just days after arriving at the club. He was also on target in a sensational 3-0 win over Paris St-Germain in the final, widely regarded as Chelsea's best moment under their current American ownership.

The Blues endured a dismal campaign following that triumph, finishing 10th in the Premier League and ending the season without a trophy and failing to qualify for Europe.

Despite that, Joao Pedro won Chelsea's player of the season award and is among a group of senior players convinced the project can succeed under Alonso.

Like midfielder Moises Caicedo and captain Reece James, he signed a new contract, while Palmer has also outlined his commitment to stay amid links with Manchester United.

All four are viewed as key culture-setters at the club.

Joao Pedro, in particular, impressed staff by giving more interviews than any other player during a season in which there were few positives to discuss.

Multiple sources have previously told BBC Sport Chelsea have a dressing-room culture problem, specifically with cliques forming along language lines.

Joao Pedro and Palmer, who count each other among their closest friends, are viewed as two of the players capable of naturally bridging those divides.

It helps that Joao Pedro has his family in the UK and has embraced aspects of local culture, having first developed an interest through his love of the Premier League. He is known to listen to trap music, a UK form of hip-hop, and both he and Palmer appeared in pop icon Madonna's promotional short film Confessions II in June.

One of Alonso's main objectives is to rebuild a wayward culture which some sources have described to BBC Sport as overly "transactional" and "cold".

After his front three, including debutant Rogers, scored against Fulham, Alonso said: "They need to take responsibility. They need to lead the rest. They need to inspire the rest because if they do great, the others will follow."

Few know how Joao Pedro handled his omission from the Brazil squad at the World Cup, where they were knocked out in the last 16 by Norway this summer.

Even those closest to him do not know how disappointed he was to miss out, given that playing for Brazil at a World Cup had long been one of his biggest dreams.

"When Joao Pedro is angry, he doesn't shout, he goes quiet," Junqueira said of his general personality.

After Chelsea's struggles season and the lack of World Cup involvement, he had two weeks completely off.

Joao Pedro spent the rest of his summer in Rio training with Goncalves, his personal fitness coach since childhood, surrounded by friends and following many of the same routines he always has.

Ultimately, according to Goncalves, the frontman remains the same person, but one intent on becoming a truly "elite".

Since returning to Chelsea in the summer, he has scored eight goals in seven pre-season matches before finding the net 31 seconds into the new campaign at Fulham.

It now appears Joao Pedro may be the one capable of finally ending talk and concern of the club's number nine curse.

SportsTab.title: Olivia Smith: £1m Arsenal striker wins second straight PFA young player award
SportsTab.text:
Olivia Smith has lived her life under a spotlight since she was 15 - but she had been preparing herself even before she became a professional footballer.

Now 22, Smith became the first £1m women's footballer last year when Arsenal signed her in a world record deal from Liverpool.

She had joined Liverpool for a club record of £210,000 just one season earlier, having made a name for herself when she was given her Canada debut aged 15.

Smith became the first woman to score for Liverpool at Anfield in a Women's Super League match in October 2025.

Now, for the second year in a row, she is the first non-English recipient of the PFA women's young player of the year award.

But how did Smith's sacrifices early in life help her reach the top?

Smith grew up in the small Canadian city of Whitby, where from a young age she was encouraged to play football by her father, Sean.

She jumped between local clubs every year and played with boys until the age of 12 before finally settling into a girls' team.

Clearly talented, she continued to train with boys at the same time, while enjoying a multi-cultural upbringing around Toronto.

"My parents have made a lot of sacrifices taking me to all these places and moving every couple of years," Smith told BBC Sport.

"My dad's Jamaican, my mom's Chilean and Peruvian. There's so much football culture within those.

"I grasped a lot of that from my dad's dad who played football and my mom's dad also played in South America. I think I have that flair in my DNA.

"Of course, I [enjoy the different] food, music, all those kinds of things. In Toronto, you find it is a very multicultural place and that was really cool growing up."

But Smith later experienced bullying and turned to different sports as coping mechanisms, not knowing at the time how it would help her football career.

"I did taekwondo as a kid. I was getting bullied in school so it was more of a defensive mechanism kind of thing," said Smith.

"I did gymnastics too. That really helps with my agility. I find that, for my stature, I'm quite flexible as well, which really helps injury prevention.

"Taekwondo really helped with my discipline and arguably my shooting ability in terms of its speed.

"I think mainly it was just to keep me active, out of trouble, and it was just for fun. Thankfully it contributed to my footballing career."

Smith also thinks the unusual sporting background helped her when dealing with attention and pressure, as well as bullying.

"It helps with just the discipline on and off the pitch in simple tasks that are really important in my day-to-day life," added Smith.

"In gymnastics, you have to do splits or planks for [a length of time]. It's really hard mentally so that helped me mature. I developed a lot of mental toughness."

It is not just Smith who has invested in football since a young age. Her dad, Sean, was tracking her statistics to monitor her progress.

"That is his favourite thing in the world to do. When I was younger, he would literally film all my games," said Smith.

"After games, we would go back and watch everything, see what I could have done better and what I did well.

"He kept a diary of the goals that I scored, what minute it was in and things like that. He still has it to this day. He loves it!"

Beyond football, Smith loves to cook and watch TV series - Law and Order: SVU is a current favourite - and she says she is "dying to get a puppy".

The young forward has learned to become independent, having left home as a teenager in order to chase a professional career.

But it hasn't been easy. When Smith moved to Michigan aged 15 on her own, she didn't know where she would be living when she boarded the plane.

"Moving around a lot, you're sacrificing relationships because you make good friends in one place, then you have to move," said Smith.

"That makes it quite tough, especially when you're young. I struggled a lot with that. I had to leave to get training elsewhere.

"It helped me get used to what was to come, so I think it was a very important sacrifice in my journey.

"I'm so grateful that I've been able to make so many connections in different places, so even though I'm away from home I feel like I have family."

For the first time in her career, Smith is about to begin a second season at the same club having settled into life at Arsenal. The Gunners begin their WSL campaign at Brighton on Sunday, 6 September (12:00 BST kick-off).

"When I stepped into the building for my second pre-season it just felt surreal. It feels like home. It feels like Arsenal's the place that's meant to be," said Smith.

"It's an honour to be here. I'm just super excited to see where it takes me. I've always wanted to be somewhere for more than a year; I've moved around so much.

"I also knew there was so much more for me and I wanted to be the best that I could be. All those moves led me here."

Smith's ambitions have not changed.

At the age of six or seven, she wrote down in a journal what she wanted to achieve.

"I had a journal with everything in it that I wanted to accomplish and what I wanted to do: I want to win the Ballon d'Or. I want to win the World Cup," she added.

"That's still the case today. I want to win trophies with [Arsenal]. I've had this mentality since I was young. It is what has driven me this far."

SportsTab.title: Celtic's Champions League defeat: Martin O'Neill takes responsibility after loss to LASK
SportsTab.text:
In the open air of the Raiffeisen Arena, with bedlam all around, there was nowhere to hide for Celtic or Martin O'Neill.

The Scottish champions had endured one of the darkest nights in their European history.

After going out to Kairat Almaty on penalties last year at this stage of the Champions League play-offs, that is saying something.

Four goals up on aggregate against LASK, O'Neill's Celtic somehow conspired to implode in a second half with little sign of a response on the way to a 5-4 aggregate loss following extra time.

There was no hiding place, and the Celtic manager was frank when put in the spotlight at full-time.

"I'm responsible for this one," he said.

"Without a doubt. Naturally it took me a long time to get over the Uefa Cup final in 2003 but this was majorly disappointing.

"In the context of things, one was a final which it would have been terrific to win, this was a qualifying game which we should have been able to get through.

"We know that we are a million miles from the finished article. That's absolutely true. I think we thought that anyway."

O'Neill was not in charge for that defeat in Kazakhstan a year ago as it triggered the start of the end for Brendan Rodgers' second spell at Celtic Park.

The current Parkhead boss helped steady Celtic's ship last term following Rodgers' exit and again following the Wilfried Nancy saga to guide them to another league title and a Scottish Cup.

This season appeared to get off to a prosperous start until the roof began to cave in over in Austria.

Away from the raw pain of stumbling in such a stark way, the aftermath could be telling for Celtic who now have to not only pick themselves up, but finish off a transfer window without the hefty windfall which would have blown in with the Champions League.

"The qualification for the Champions League is major, it's major in every aspect," said O'Neill.

"Financially, for prestige, but we have to pick ourselves up. That's my responsibility again to do that.

"I think I said last week that if you could qualify for the Champions League there would be players wanting to come on that basis.

"That's not going to be the case but we'll see. Tonight we came up well and truly short, particularly in the second half."

Celtic captain Callum McGregor tells Amazon Prime: "We got what we deserved. We were passive all night. We looked scared to go and win the game.

"I didn't think we were that good in the first leg either. We scored at good times and got away with it.

"We have to suck it up. We apologise to our supporters and the club because there's no way we should lose that game.

"It's as much on the players as everyone else. You can't look for excuses elsewhere.

"You'll now see what people are made of. When you play like that you can't have any excuses whatsoever.

"When you go 1-0 up in the game and it still doesn't settle you, you can't have any excuse and that's on us.

"You fall at a big hurdle and these questions [on whether the squad are ready] are going to be asked. You can't lose by that margin then look for excuses elsewhere.

"This is what it's like to play at Celtic. You have to bounce back, you have to show a reaction and that's what Celtic are all about."

SportsTab.title: Mikaela Mayer vs Chantelle Cameron: Five years from influencers to queens of women's boxing for upstart promoters
SportsTab.text:
On 29 August, one of the feistiest upstarts in modern boxing will celebrate a fifth anniversary.

On the same date in 2021, Most Valuable Promotions' headline bout for its inaugural show in Cleveland, Ohio, featured co-founder and online influencer Jake Paul taking on MMA fighter Tyron Woodley in the boxing ring.

MVP's second event, just under four months later in Tampa, Florida, was a Paul-Woodley rematch.

For a long time, MVP's most notable event featured Paul - regarded as the face of YouTuber boxing - fighting Mike Tyson.

It came at a time when Tyson was so far over the hill that the hill could not be seen in the rearview mirror.

MVP's reputation developed as it put together cards with names and output that were anathema to boxing purists.

The five-year anniversary card, however, shows a side of MVP which has emerged alongside what some would consider its gaudiness.

And perhaps what takes place this weekend offers a better indication of the promotion's future than the fights that have gone before.

The main card features five women's bouts, headlined by Mikaela Mayer taking on Chantelle Cameron to unify the WBA, WBC and WBO light-middleweight belts.

The primary support will showcase Caroline Dubois defending her WBC and WBO lightweight titles against Amelia Moore.

MVP, for years dismissed by critics as a snot-nosed upstart of promotion, could now be regarded as a major player and the primary UK promoter of women's boxing.

"Respect, I think, is the biggest change. I've seen and felt it," Dubois told BBC Sport.

"I remember coming into the scene of the sporting world and if you say you're a female boxer, people will look at you like 'ah' – but now people are like 'OK, let's see you fight' – it's not a joke, a gimmick, a side caricature. It's part of the real deal."

Fellow Briton Cameron left promoter Queensberry for MVP last year.

Her WBC interim title fight against Patricia Berghult in November 2024 had been a co-main event at Birmingham's BP Pulse Arena.

Eight months later, Cameron fought Jessica Camara at New York's iconic Madison Square Garden.

She returns to the BP Pulse on Saturday, this time in the outright headline fight for her biggest bout since a 2023 double-header against Katie Taylor.

"MVP are taking over women's boxing," Cameron told BBC Sport. "They've been amazing. Everything they've said they'll do, they've done.

"They got me my world title shot. They got me my Mayer fight. It's all been so quick – it's just my third fight with them."

Before her spell with Queenberry, Cameron had been on Matchroom's books. She beat Taylor in their first fight, before the Irish superstar avenged the defeat second time around.

"The Katie Taylor fights were great fights and both will always go down in history," she said. "But it dipped. I lost momentum. Went on the shelf. I couldn't get the names, couldn't get the fights, nobody wanted to fight me. I wanted the fights, but they just weren't happening."

Dubois, Cameron, Mayer and Terri Harper are among the top women's boxing talent signed to MVP.

Serrano, Alycia Baumgardner and former undisputed super-bantamweight champion Ellie Scotney are also on board.

So why is MVP the go-to promoter for such female boxing talent?

Dubois has developed a brash new persona since working with MVP - calling out Harper before her previous bout before some verbal sparring led to a feisty face-off.

Tacky? Some might think so. But it saw Dubois move from fighting at the tiny Park Community Arena in Sheffield to Miami and London's Olympia.

"They've helped me get to that next level," Dubois says. "I want to be involved in the best, the biggest and the most important fights in boxing.

"Jake [Paul] brings the social influencer dynamic. He gave me tips and pointers and how I should build these fights.

"We're entertainers, that's what we are. It's always good to get that insight from someone who is technically outside of the sport. He has that fresh mindset. MVP have that on lock."

While Dubois defends her titles on Saturday, Harper, who lost their April bout on points, begins her rebuild earlier on the card against Miranda Reyes.

Harper considered retirement after losing to Sandy Ryan in 2024, but she had no such thoughts after defeat to Dubois.

"I'm nearly 30 now and I now really want to enjoy it," Harper told BBC Sport. "It's my last roll of the dice to see how far I can push to become a four-weight world champion.

"MVP have delivered the fights I want, and a greater audience."

MVP looks to balance its serious stance on women's boxing with its influencer roots - August plans featured an 'MVP x Tiktok Live' event, starring Serrano.

There is no doubt that if MVP is to keep up its momentum in women's sport, the arena events and headline acts have to stay.

"I remember my first amateur fight in Camden, or walking into the gym when I was nine years old at Repton," Dubois says.

"Now I'm fighting there and I'm talking about headlining and talking about fighting on Netflix."

If there is one thing an organisation led by Paul can provide, it is talk and spectacle.

For Cameron and Mayer, MVP has the chance to make a real difference in women's boxing.

"I'm an advocate for three-minute rounds," says Cameron. "We've got a long way to go, but if more women started doing what the men do, we can start saying they give us the opportunity for equality for women's boxing."

Fighters like Cameron and Mayer have memories that go back beyond the dawn of MVP. They know how their sport has struggled, and know the work still needed.

"In order for a sport to develop, they need to compete and women are a step behind because we weren't allowed to even compete in the Olympics until 2012," says Mayer.

"It's not going to happen overnight, but this is what we needed to take women's boxing to the next step."

TechnologyTab.title: GTA 6 leaks: Rockstar issues statement over online clips
TechnologyTab.text:
Grand Theft Auto 6 maker Rockstar Games has issued a statement addressing a series of leaked videos showing the upcoming blockbuster video game.

Clips appearing to show gameplay and cinematics from the title began appearing online last week, but the developer did not acknowledge them straight away.

In a statement, the company said the leaks had been "heartbreaking" for the team working on the sequel, and that they were "not how we intended for you to see the game after all this time".

The company apologised for the delays in releasing official updates on the highly anticipated title, but vowed to "exceed" fans' expectations in a special preview airing on Netflix this week.

When leaks first began to surface, there was some doubt as to whether they were genuine.

But as the days went on, evidence mounted to suggest they were legitimate.

Copies of clips were quickly taken down from social media sites via copyright strikes, where the owner of a work can request its removal.

And, on Friday, Rockstar's parent company Take Two Interactive launched legal proceedings regarding the leaks in a New York court.

Rockstar acknowledged players had been waiting for it to address the leaked footage, and said it was "unfortunate the intended game experience may now be impacted by some spoilers".

It also thanked fans who sent messages of support over the past week, adding: "Your words have meant more to the team than you can imagine."

The group behind the leaks claims to be acting in the interests of players, accusing Rockstar of engaging in anti-consumer practices such as its decision not to release a disc version of GTA 6 at launch.

Not everyone is convinced, as each release of new material has invited viewers to send cryptocurrency "donations" to the user uploading them.
