EntertainmentTab.title: From Jolene to Islands in the Stream: Dolly Parton’s 10 best recordings
EntertainmentTab.text:
The death of Dolly Parton today at age 80 has the world mourning one of America’s most beloved entertainers: a generation-spanning performer and country music icon who took as much pride in her music as she did her sparkling appearance. Parton’s impressive musical output across a 60-year career and a whopping 50 albums was built on a foundation of her undeniable knack for songwriting: ranging from heartfelt lyrics to catchy hooks. Here are just 10 of Parton’s greatest contributions to the American musical lexicon.

It’s a country classic that straddles the line between tough and vulnerable, and according to an oft-told story by Parton, inspired by true events. Based on a real person Parton felt threatened by that her late husband Carl Dean knew, the music legend turned her anxiety into some of the sharpest lines of her career which hum along on an unforgettable melody. As legend has it, the real person was a red-headed clerk at a local bank. Meanwhile, the actual name came from a young fan she signed an autograph for; the chorus came from Parton repeating Jolene over and over so she wouldn’t later forget it. Landing on multiple lists that rank the greatest songs of all time, Jolene also holds the distinction of being nominated for a Grammy for best female country vocal performance twice: once for the original track in 1975, and then again for a live recording a year later.

I Will Always Love You (1974)

Demonstrating Parton’s undeniable knack for songwriting, one of the most amazing stories in the annals of music history is that Parton wrote Jolene and her tour de force romantic anthem I Will Always Love You within a stunningly short span of each other. (The previous legend stated that she wrote them on the same day, which Parton humbly disputed in 2022). Funnily enough, Parton didn’t write this one in tribute to her husband: instead, it was an ode to mentor Porter Wagoner, with Parton penning the track in light of going solo after closely collaborating with the fellow country icon. “If I should stay, I would only be in your way,” she memorably croons as the song opens. Sure, fellow icon Whitney Houston would later make the song her own, but Parton’s version is just as legendary.

Get that steaming cup of ambition! It’s a working-class anthem for the ages, and Parton makes the office grind sound kind of fun. Recorded for the 1980 comedy 9 to 5 which starred Parton alongside Lily Tomlin and Jane Fonda as hard workers with an ax to, well, grind, both the blockbuster movie and song launched Parton firmly into the mainstream upon its release. The bouncy tune kicks off with that pulsating piano, almost mimicking a machine, before busting into its instantly memorable chorus and it was all inspired by her nails. On set, Parton would scrape her acrylics together, with the rhythm and beat born out of a unique movement only Parton could concoct. The 9 to 5 track itself became Parton’s first Hot 100 No 1 hit, and it would later inspire a 2009 musical.

Coat of Many Colors (1971)

Any fan of Parton knows about her hardscrabble youth; growing up in poverty in the mountains of rural Tennessee before she evolved into the dazzling legend we know her as today. Parton never forgot those humble beginnings and would share her inspirational story in a series of projects throughout her life. That includes her signature song Coat of Many Colors which was inspired by a chilly Tennessee fall back in the day. “I recall a box of rags that someone gave us, and how my momma put the rags to use,” she delicately sings in the tender ode ripped from her childhood. “Momma sewed the rags together, sewin’ every piece with love, she made my coat of many colors, I was so proud of.” OK, where are the tissues?

Islands in the Stream (1983)

Take one listen to Islands in the Stream and it will be impossible to get the earworm out of your head. Holding the distinction as Parton’s second-ever Hot 100 No 1 hit, on Islands in the Stream she’s paired perfectly with the country crooner Kenny Rogers on the sweet and smooth track which bubbles along much like its eponymous waterway. The song is also an outlier in Parton’s discography, as it’s one of a handful of trademark songs she didn’t write. (The Bee Gees, Barry, Maurice and Robin Gibb, are credited on this one). Nevertheless, the combination of all five unique personalities turned the bouncy track into one of the best duets of all time and a bona fide karaoke staple.

Here You Come Again (1977)

In addition to Islands in the Stream, Here You Come Again is another rare track Parton didn’t pen. Here You Come Again, her first gold record, was penned by Brill Building legends Barry Mann and Cynthia Weil, with the buoyant ditty sounding like such a surefire hit to Parton, she was reluctant to record it. “She said a monkey could sing this song and have a hit with it,” her manager Sandy Gallin said in 2016. “And she was very nervous that it would turn off the country market, which she was very loyal to. There was no way she wanted to ever let anything insinuate that she may be turning her back on the country audience.” Parton need not have worried: country fans embraced the tune so much that it lodged five weeks at No 1 on the country charts, later winning a Grammy.

Two Doors Down (1978)

Deftly mixing Parton’s country twang with the panache of pop, further evidence of Parton’s crossover success between the two genres can be heard on Two Doors Down, which continues Jolene’s themes of loneliness. Lyrically, she portrayed an isolated woman whose lover is having a brouhaha right down the hall. Oddly enough, as Parton told Kelly Clarkson in 2022, it was inspired by a diet Parton was on at the time. She and her band were staying at a Howard Johnson’s Motor Lodge. But while her band was feasting on fried clams and having a good ol’ time, Parton sulking in her room, sticking to only consuming liquid protein. “I could hear them all laughing and talking, and I just started singing: two doors down, they’re laughing and drinking and having a party,” she recalled.

Why’d You Come in Here Lookin’ Like That? (1989)

Marking Parton’s 22nd No 1 on the country charts upon its late-80s release, Why’d You Come In Here Lookin’ Like That? is classic Parton, with the energetic track dripping with the attitude and sass she will forever be known for. The first to crack a joke about her appearance (her favorite saying: “It costs a lot of money to look this cheap”), Parton was proudly vain and widely extravagant in her looks, from her fashion, nails and hair. Naturally, she would strike a chord with a song where she flips the narrative, criticizing a fellow gal about her own appearance flaunting “cowboy boots and your painted-on jeans, all decked out like a cowgirl’s dream”. The only thing sharper than Parton’s looks was her tongue.

Most artists slow down, peter out, sell out and offer diminished returns as the decades trudge on. Parton, meanwhile, was roaring on all cylinders into her 70s, with the superstar continually releasing an array of unique new projects. Her last full album was 2023’s Rockstar, a cover album which saw Parton duet with everyone from goddaughter Miley Cyrus to Paul McCartney and Elton John on a fun and silly series of rock’n’roll covers. Parton, however, had to put her own mark on the project, writing a title track that opens up the melodic bacchanal. Starting with a thrashing guitar courtesy Richie Sambora, Rockstar symbolizes her generation-spanning relevance and a passionate devotion to pure creativity.

If You Hadn’t Been There (2025)

Perhaps it’s fitting that one of the very last singles Parton released during her eight decades was last spring’s If You Hadn’t Been There, a tearjerker love song to her beloved husband who died the week before. “If you hadn’t been there, where would I be?” Parton lusciously asks in her unmistakable whisper-tone as a piano tickles in the background. The late-career song is a perfect example of Parton’s access to unbridled emotion: as much as she was unafraid to let her hair down, she was also fearlessly vulnerable and emotive. As an artist, that yin and yang is a golden encapsulation of what made her so special. And now, legions of music fans are asking the same question about Dolly herself: if you hadn’t been there, where would we be?

EntertainmentTab.title: Dolly Parton’s peerless career turned country music cliches inside out
EntertainmentTab.text:
In December 1977, Dolly Parton submitted to an interview with ABC Television’s Barbara Walters, much against her friends’ advice. Walters was not noted for her deep love and understanding of country music. She was a notoriously tough cookie, a Boston-born, Sarah Lawrence-educated journalist who had battled scarcely believable sexism to become the first female co-host of an American news programme. The month before she met Parton, she had interviewed Anwar Sadat and Menachem Begin while they were working out the terms of the Egypt-Israel peace treaty.

It was all a very long way from Parton’s world, and the interview has something of the anthropological exercise about it. Walters looks aghast as Parton shows her around her tour bus, her collection of wigs and her “hand-washable and wrinkle-free” stage outfits (“you really like this? To me, it seems like horror”), and sits impassively as Parton sings Coat of Many Colours to her: an impressive feat, given the song’s saga of rural poverty and homespun wisdom is the mother of all tearjerkers from an artist never averse to yanking at her audience’s heartstrings. She asks Parton if people from “where I come from” would call her a hillbilly; regards the singer’s outfit with a jaundiced eye and tells her “you don’t have to look like this”. And, most infamously, she enquires: “Do you ever feel that you’re a joke?”

“The joke’s on the public,” responds Parton, her smile never slipping. “I know exactly what I’m doing and I can change it any time … I’m sure of myself. I’m sure of my talent.”

It was a TV appearance that told you a lot about public perceptions of Parton in the years when she surged from Nashville fame to international superstardom – an era when you could turn on British TV and find a Canadian duo called MacLean and MacLean performing a mocking song called Dolly Parton’s Tits – and also told you a lot about Parton herself, most notably that, beneath the wig and the rhinestones, she had rather more in common with Walters than anyone might have thought.

Of course she was sure of her talent: by the time she sat down with Walters, she had already written a string of imperishable country standards: not just Coat of Many Colours, but Jolene, My Tennessee Mountain Home, Down from Dover, I Will Always Love You, Little Bird, Kentucky Gambler, Love Is Like a Butterfly, The Bargain Store, The Seeker. Of course she knew exactly what she was doing with her image, based – as she never tired of telling interviewers – on “the town tramp” back in Pittman Center, Tennessee. A woman whose first solo hit was called Dumb Blonde, she used it both to lure in a certain type of country fan (“rednecks with flat tops who bring women who wear short skirts or tight pants,” as one 1970s journalist sniffily put it) and as a kind of glitzy, fluffy shield.

Behind it, she could be subtly subversive. Years before the controversy around Loretta Lynn’s 1975 single The Pill highlighted the issue of Nashville’s sexism, Parton was writing songs of a distinctly feminist bent – Just Because I’m a Woman and When Possession Gets Too Strong among them – even if she always demurred from describing herself as such. She also had a line in songs that could give more conservative Nashville stars palpitations. Down from Dover was extraordinarily beautiful, but it seemed to simmer with empathic rage on behalf of its protagonist, an outcast unmarried mother, and concluded with a description of her giving birth to a stillborn baby. Her duet partner Porter Wagoner was so horrified that he urged her not to release it: she did, and it was summarily banned by country radio.

And behind her image, she could be a model of smart, steely self-determination. If the country music establishment had a tendency to look down on her (the songwriter Tom T Hall once noted that he and Kris Kristofferson were the only two people in Nashville “who could describe Dolly Parton without using their hands”), she was abundantly aware of her own worth. The then-more-famous Wagoner was doing her a favour in 1967 when he adopted her as his duet partner, but Parton did most of the heavy lifting when it came to the pair’s songwriting, and left when it became apparent her success was beginning to outstrip his, occasioning a $3m lawsuit in the process. Moreover, she famously turned down Elvis Presley’s overtures to record the heart-rending song she wrote about the duo’s split, I Will Always Love You, when Presley’s manager indicated he wanted a cut of the songwriting royalties in return.

She was clearly possessed of a far greater artistic and commercial ambition than she was given credit for. The former was evidenced by 1973’s My Tennessee Mountain Home, an entirely self-penned autobiographical concept album that was rather less sentimental in its recollections than you might expect: “No amount of money could pay me to go back and live through it again,” she sang of her poverty-stricken rural upbringing on In the Good Old Days (When Times Were Bad). It ranks among the best things she ever released. Her daring became apparent around the time of the Walters interview, when Parton made a lunge for the pop mainstream, disregarding fears that it would alienate her existing audience.

She scored a succession of huge pop hits: 1977’s Mann and Weill-penned Here You Come Again went to No 3 on the Hot 100, a chart on which Jolene had, incredibly, only peaked at No 60; three years later 9 to 5 hit No 1. She also transformed into an actor and dabbled in disco without losing her country essence. During her quest for mainstream success, she was as likely to essay a bluegrass version of the Beatles’ Help!, or a cover of Woody Guthrie’s Deportee (Plane Wreck at Los Gatos), or unleash upon the world Me and Little Andy, a song that anywhere other than Nashville would be regarded as a bit much – a child and a puppy snuff it in the final verse – as she was to release the winningly high-camp disco of Potential New Boyfriend. She really did know exactly what she was doing.

In a sense, her moment as a mainstream crossover pop star was relatively short-lived. There was one more huge hit with 1983’s peerless Islands in the Stream, a Bee Gees-penned duet with Kenny Rodgers, but that moment had drawn to close by the time of 1987’s Rainbow. It seemed Parton had reached her limit with trying to cater to a broad audience – doggedly ploughing her way through its written-to-order contents, she sounded bored stiff, particularly when compared with the same year’s superb Trio, a collaboration with Emmylou Harris and Linda Ronstadt.

And besides, Rainbow’s commercial failure didn’t matter. Perhaps because she had never really turned her back on country – 1984’s Tennessee Homesick Blues opened with sound of Parton yodelling – Nashville welcomed her full-blooded return to the genre, with 1989’s Ricky Skaggs-produced White Limozeen. If she never scored another US Hot 100 hit, the broader celebrity she had established in the late 70s and early 80s never waned for the rest of her life. Tellingly, while promoting White Limozeen’s standout track, the insanely catchy and uproariously funny Why’d You Come in Here Lookin’ Like That?, she hosted Saturday Night Live: it would be a decade before another country star did so.

In truth, Parton’s subsequent albums were of a decidedly mixed quality, at least until she returned to absolute basics: 1999’s Grammy-winning The Grass Is Blue kicked off a trio of stark, fantastic albums that dealt in bluegrass, Appalachian folk and country gospel, the music that she had “grown up surrounded by”. Thereafter, what she put out was hit-and-and miss: misjudged horrors including 2003’s post-9/11 collection of patriotic songs, For God and Country, abutting albums as good as 2014’s Blue Smoke, although her voice sounded magnificent no matter the material. She was still more than capable of writing fantastic songs – but nothing that could eclipse the best of her 70s material.

It didn’t really matter, because the best of her 70s material had long taken on a life of its own outside country music. Whitney Houston’s cover of I Will Always Love You became the biggest-selling single of all time by a female artist. At the last count, Jolene has been covered nearly 90 times: you could hear it rendered as noisy alt-rock by the White Stripes, synth-pop by Strawberry Switchblade, or a dubby post-club soundtrack by One Dove.

Meanwhile, in the 21st century, the full extent of Parton’s influence on pop became apparent. Younger stars queued up to pay homage of one kind or another. Taylor Swift, who knows a thing or two about pivoting away from country to pop, called her “a force of evolution and transformation in our industry”. Parton co-wrote Rainbowland on her goddaughter Miley Cyrus’s 2017 album Younger Now, and you didn’t have to analyse Sabrina Carpenter’s work too deeply to spot the influence. The fact that Carpenter’s 2024 smash Please Please Please sounded like something Parton might have written evidently didn’t escape Parton herself: she turned up duetting with Carpenter on a remixed version of the song, the swearing decorously omitted.

As fans of Tammy Wynette or Patsy Cline would be quick to point out, Parton certainly wasn’t the first female country star to cross over into the pop charts, but she nevertheless seemed like the godmother of the pop-country that has swept the charts in recent years, which one Spotify playlist characterised as “Neon Cowgirl” (Parton was by far the oldest artist to make said playlist, rubbing shoulders with Swift, Carpenter, Chappell Roan, Kesha et al). When Beyoncé made a musical leap into country on Cowboy Carter, it somehow seemed inevitable that Parton would be involved, and so it proved: she delivered a spoken-word introduction to Beyoncé’s redux of Jolene. In fact, she seemed as present in pop music in the mid-2020s as she had been in the late 70s. The difference was that no one would have asked her if she was a joke. That question had been answered to everyone’s satisfaction a long time ago.

EntertainmentTab.title: ‘We met Princess Margaret and she was paralytic!’ My wild life onboard the Adam and the Ants Antmania rollercoaster
EntertainmentTab.text:
‘The essence of pop is, one, brilliant fucking songs – and the rest is sex, subversion, style and humour. And that was us.” So Adam Ant told me in 1995, describing the reconstructed Adam and the Ants, which formed in early 1980 with the arrival of guitarist/songwriter Marco Pirroni, who was sitting next to him. “We’re responsible for bringing back dressing up, going mad and screaming your head off.”

“That’s it!” grins Pirroni when I remind him of this, as we sit in the shabby-chic lounge of London’s 21Soho venue. Back then, I didn’t tell them I was 15 in 1980, forever sprinting across dancefloors pretending to be Adam Ant, chiffon scarves tied to knees, limbs flailing like a whirling Cossack. Pirroni hears this today and laughs. “That’s what it’s all about,” he hoots. “When I was 13, watching Bowie, Roxy, T Rex, you just go, ‘I wanna do that.’ It’s exciting, sexy, about looking good, Top of the Pops. I can’t imagine anyone saying, ‘Wow, I desperately want to be in Cabaret Voltaire. They must be earning no money, look boring and nobody likes them – that’s the band for me!’”

Pirroni, 67, is a winningly wry character, his sardonic eye enlivening his rollicking memoir, Your Money or Your Life: From Punk to Prince Charming. The book leads us, in forensic detail, through his teen years in mid-to-late 70s London. He was involved in every aspect of punk, every character, clothes shop, incident, ludicrous look and iconic gig. He was also a friend and bandmate of Sid Vicious, temporary guitarist with Siouxsie and the Banshees – and was obsessed with Roxy Music, John Barry and the spaghetti western soundtrack thrills of Ennio Morricone.

These were the sensibilities he brought to the newly adrift Adam Ant in late 1979, after three original Ants were stolen by estranged manager Malcolm McLaren for new proteges Bow Wow Wow. They informed the Ants’ landmark second album, Kings of the Wild Frontier, released in November 1980 and mostly written in Pirroni’s bedroom in his parents’ home in Harrow, London. The pair conjured a feat of audacious imagination, a call-to-arms cacophony of twangy guitars, lusty yodelling, voodoo incantations, comedy gunshots and euphoric, communal chanting.

Underpinning everything was their pioneering, two-drummer, Burundi beat sound. This was first suggested by McLaren, as was Native American imagery, and the result was a band that looked like a charging tribe of invincible warriors thundering over the horizon, fronted by a pirouetting pirate in feathers-and-frills, an “Apache” white stripe slashed across his nose.

The impact was rapid, global and era-defining: Kings of the Wild Frontier wasn’t just No 1 in the album charts for 12 weeks, the band’s singles and narrative videos – storyboarded by Ant – laid the theatrical, visual-pop foundations for MTV in the US in 1981. They were dastardly, suggestive and definitely grownup, but they nonetheless ignited primal stirrings in even preteens, who saw in Ant a supernaturally attractive superhero, even before his turns as glossy-lipped Dandy Highwayman and pompadoured Prince Charming.

Ant wore glasses: thick-lensed, National Health whoppers. The first night Pirroni saw him without them on, wearing that white nose stripe and dressed in the 19th-century, gold-braided Hussar jacket from the film The Charge of the Light Brigade, his appeal was obvious. “It was like Clark Kent becoming Superman,” says Pirroni, who cultivated his own look, fond of polka dots and skull and crossbones. The band travelled with three huge wardrobe trunks. “And one was just my stuff!” says Pirroni.

Today, the Ants’ Native American leanings would ignite accusations of cultural appropriation. But Pirroni rejects this. “Culture belongs to the human race,” he asserts. “It’s not even stealing. It’s ideas – they’re free. It’s art. We tried to do it well. We didn’t take the piss! Well, I’m going to be dead soon so it doesn’t really matter what I think. You go off and create your own thing. Or steal somebody else’s thing or whatever the fuck you want.”

For 18 months of Antmania, life moved at cosmic speed, a flip book of TV shows, hotels and airports, a heady era for deadly, disparate pop rivals. Pirroni was friends or acquainted with an ostentation of peacocking characters: from his punk years (Billy Idol, Viv Albertine, Chrissie Hynde), his Blitz Club-going era (Steve Strange, Spandau Ballet), and the ones he’d bump into at airports (Culture Club, Duran Duran, the Stray Cats, Madness). “Lots of people I knew personally were on telly, getting successful,” he nods. “And we’re probably all thinking, ‘Those bastards!’ You’re young, you’re supposed to be competitive. I used to say in the press, ‘Their record’s shit!’ That’s the way bands are.”

Soon life became absurd. The Ants were regulars on kids’ TV: Tiswas, Multi-Coloured Swap Shop, The Children’s Royal Variety Performance with Clive Dunn, Basil Brush, Rod Hull and Emu. “Adam really thought Rod Hull and Emu were going to attack him,” he laughs. “Princess Margaret was completely paralytic, breathing on you. We found it all hilariously funny. The pirate ship that seemingly took us up the Hudson in New York? It wasn’t a magnificent pirate ship with skull and crossbones. It was this stupid Playmobil … cartoon. As much as we were trying to be a cartoon – but not like this!”

They had dinner with Liza Minnelli, hung out backstage with Liberace. “I remember being in this great big James Bond-like hotel suite looking over Tokyo and saying to Adam, ‘How did we get here?’ Eighteen months before, we’d been in my bedroom in Harrow.”

Their descent was equally rapid. By late 1981, the band had three managers and Ant’s erratic personality – prone to excessive drama, persistent paranoia and chart-success obsession – was increasingly problematic. “Adam is extremely difficult,” declares Pirroni. “It was always, ‘Oh God, what now?’ ‘The BBC’s banned our record.’ ‘No, they haven’t, they’re just not playing it.’”

By the age of just 22, Pirroni was disillusioned. He hated performing, finding it “boring, repetitive” and felt exasperated over all the infighting and resentments. “Bands are not built to last,” he says. As the Prince Charming Revue tour ended in January 1982, a cynical quip from Ant finished Pirroni off.

“He said, ‘No one cares what we sound like, they just want to see me dance about.’ I thought, ‘Well, fuck it, what am I doing here then?’ It did feel a bit like the Beatles – with a really, really young audience, young girls. We didn’t do that on purpose. Perhaps we were just completely infantile!”

Their relationship endured after the split in March 1982, lasting throughout the 80s and 90s, with Pirroni also working with Sinéad O’Connor and Siobhan Fahey, the Bananarama founder who is now a close friend (they’ve holidayed together in Antigua).

Today, Adam Ant still tours, having been diagnosed with bipolar disorder. As a young man, he had mental health issues, which Pirroni was aware of in the 80s but remained a little sceptical “because he does make things up”. During the 1990s, he fielded calls from Ant’s doctors, the police and his neighbours: “I didn’t blame him. He was sick.”

He was with Ant the day of his infamous altercation in the Prince of Wales pub in Kentish Town in 2002, wielding a starting pistol at revellers who mocked his cowboy outfit. He was later charged with affray and sectioned. Beforehand, Pirroni and Ant had met up in a restaurant, but Ant bolted off to continue drinking, says Pirroni. In the 1980s, the singer had famously been a righteous teetotaller in a hedonistic era. His disciplined lifestyle was, explains Pirroni today, a reaction to his severely alcoholic father. “But he controlled it. Until the mania took over.”

Pirroni, who now lives a rural life in Derbyshire, lost contact with Ant years ago and is no longer interested in creating music. “Records now,” he says, “are like a plastic animal you give away with cornflakes. Your album given away to get people to come and see you live. I’m not going back on the road. You’d have to pay me millions.”

He’s done enough anyway, I assure him. For teenagers like me, what he did was magic. “I find that really hard to accept,” he unexpectedly confesses. “When someone comes up to me and says, ‘Kings is my favourite album. It really affected me.’ If I think that our album, my album, affected them in the same way as, say, Roxy Music’s For Your Pleasure affected me, then I’m scared.”

EntertainmentTab.title: ‘It destroyed me’ – your top true crime TV shows of all time
EntertainmentTab.text:
Unsolved: The Boy Who Disappeared (2016)

I watched the BBC’s Unsolved: The Boy Who Disappeared when it came out and Damien Nettles, its subject, still pops up in my mind sometimes. It’s a comprehensive, empathetic and gripping investigation into a case I had never heard of. The Serial/Making a Murderer-style approach of showing the investigation, rather than just presenting information, gives the series a much more human angle. I thought it might turn up new evidence; that level of faith in the work being shown is a testament to how thorough it was. AJ, Devon, UK

Murder on a Sunday Morning (2001)

I remember watching this with my dad. It came on TV late, as part of the Storyville strand, when I was about 20 and working in a pub, living at home. We were captivated by this story about a wrongly accused Black teenager and his trial for allegedly shooting an older white woman. It opened my eyes to police corruption, mistaken identity in lineups and the deep-rooted racism that underlies them. The accused boy is so incredibly normal, like friends of mine at the time, or my younger brother – and the impossibility that he decided to rob and shoot someone on a Sunday morning seems obvious. It is a beautiful piece of sensitive, non-sensationalist film-making with humanity at its heart. Rose, Wakefield, UK

I’m not a fan of true crime TV, but I did see the outrageous Tiger King and found it immensely watchable. Big-cat enthusiast Joe Exotic – who was jailed for animal abuse and two counts of attempted murder for hire, for plotting to kill a rival feline conservationist, Carole Baskin – is the kind of over-the-top character who seems as if he had sprung from a work of fiction. Bruce, Florida, US

Devil in the Family: the Fall of Ruby Franke (2025)

To call this a favourite is maybe not the right word; it’s the story of the family vlogger Ruby Franke and the the severe child abuse she committed. The camera footage – the story unfolding before us – made the documentary about this unforgivable crime difficult, albeit engaging, to watch. It’s horrific seeing educated people punishing children in a very cruel way. It helped to know before watching that the two perpetrators were jailed. Judith, Tyne and Wear, UK

Hometown: A Killing (2019)

This series, which focused on a murder in journalist Mobeen Azhar’s hometown of Huddersfield, was fantastic. Starting with the investigation of a single crime, the story evolves unexpectedly into a really interesting dive into societal and cultural issues, and Azhar’s personal connection to the place means he is clearly invested. It’s one of the best explorations of crime in modern Britain that I’ve seen and it’s available on BBC iPlayer. Neil Marshall, 43, Glasgow, UK

Confessions With a Killer: The Ted Bundy Tapes (2019)

I watched Confessions With a Killer: The Ted Bundy Tapes for the first time with a friend during my first year of uni – and then maybe 100 times since. It’s the high-water mark of an anthology series that also featured Charles Manson and John Wayne Gacy, balancing the sensational and truthful admirably, and giving due respect to the victims. It also allows Bundy to continually dob himself in, emphasising his monstrous ego and lack of empathy. Psychologically and in highlighting the police successes and failures, I still find it fascinating. It’s led to a lifelong fascination with true crime. Issy, 27, London, UK

Dear Zachary: A Letter to a Son About His Father (2008)

I saw this about 15 years ago on a Thursday afternoon when I was off sick from work. It destroyed me. My girlfriend (now wife) came home to find me in floods of tears over the amazing David and Kathleen Bagby and how they dealt with the murder of their son, Andrew, and then the murder-suicide of his former partner, Shirley Turner (the main suspect in Andrew’s death), and one-year-old baby son, Zachary. I made everyone watch it, with the caveat that it will make you cry uncontrollably. Even typing this now, it’s making me teary, not least as it was made by Kurt Kuenne – a close friend of Andrew’s. John Fitzgerald, 58, Manchester, UK

The Staircase (2022)

The Staircase first appealed to me for its intimate view into a family in crisis. It’s a dramatisation, starring Colin Firth and Toni Collette, of a French documentary that first aired in 2004, about the case of an American novelist accused of murdering his wife (but who he claims fell down the stairs). From there, the rollercoaster progresses – slowly but no less exhilaratingly. The sentiments go from “there are just too many coincidences, he must be guilty”, to “he may be guilty, but the evidence is shoddy at best”, to “even if he is guilty, the American justice system is the real bad guy here and he should never have been convicted”, to ultimately believing that he probably is innocent. As a brother to a criminal defence lawyer, I always prefer true crime that helps unjustly convicted people. The Staircase is a great example of that. Michiel Pauw, 38, Amsterdam, the Netherlands

OJ: Made in America (2016)

OJ: Made in America is such a great journey, using the story of OJ Simpson’s life, career and crimes to explain the history of modern civil rights in America. At the end of the series, you feel so captivated by the intertwining themes that you need time to synthesise it all. It’s a well put together series that shows the antecedents to broader societal trends. Anonymous, Australia

This is a Robbery: The World’s Biggest Art Heist (2021)

This is a Robbery is an in-depth look at the Isabella Stewart Gardner museum heist in Boston in 1990. It remains unsolved and the artwork has never been found. It’s really well done and digs into all the weirdness and oddities that were part of the crime. What makes it especially wild is that Isabella Gardner’s will meant that the paintings couldn’t be replaced – so to this day, the spaces on the wall remain empty. JoseRamirez, 55, Tewksbury, Massachusetts, US

The Jinx: The Life and Deaths of Robert Durst (2015)

The Jinx is probably the greatest true crime TV show of the modern era, certainly since Errol Morris’s The Thin Blue Line. Durst – who was suspected of killing his first wife, and was convicted for the murder of a friend and then a neighbour in 2000-01 – is a remarkable subject: a manipulative Jekyll and Hyde-type figure clearly with a great capacity for violence, but charismatic and vulnerable with it, and who is finally undone by his own entitlement and hubris. Watching him ignore the advice of his lawyers and wander inexorably into self-incrimination is highly entertaining. Andrew Jarecki is a fantastic storyteller, and the story itself unfolds with all the twists and turns to keep you completely engrossed. What it demonstrates about what wealth does to people, and how it leverages the legal system, is instructive. Combine all this with the jaw-dropping final reveal and it is about as good as true crime gets! Yvette, Bristol, UK

Unsolved Mysteries (1987–2010)

Unsolved Mysteries is the granddaddy of the true crime TV genre. Robert Stack was the perfect host (when he died in 2003, Dennis Farina took take over hosting duties until the end of its first run), spinning intriguing and sometimes wild and weird mysteries that you wished you could help solve. I’m sure that series helped inspire many of the armchair internet sleuths that popped up in the decades that followed. Robert Graves, 58, Los Angeles, US

The Keepers (2017)

The Keepers explores the unsolved murder of Sister Catherine Cesnik in 1969, after she grew to suspect that a priest at the Catholic high school she taught at in Baltimore had sexually abused students. This was the first true crime documentary that caught my attention. I watched and rewatched it several times, perhaps because I lived in the area in Maryland where the case happened. Susan Wilt, New York, US

American Murder: The Family Next Door (2020)

My favourite crime series has to be American Murder: The Family Next Door on Netflix. The way it’s filmed is equally enthralling and infuriating. The effect of Chris Watts’s attempts to cover up the murder of his pregnant wife and children in the town of Frederick, Colorado, in 2018 is chilling. You feel so much for his late wife, as one horrible man goes on a tear to change his life. Dane Klingaman, 40, Phoenixville, Pennsylvania, US

Last Stop Larrimah (2023)

EntertainmentTab.title: Clive Barker’s Hellraiser: Revival – a game so grotesque it scares its own director
EntertainmentTab.text:
If a horror game gives its own director a physical reaction, it’s probably doing something right. While researching the images people find hardest to look at, game director Emil Esov discovered he has trypophobia – a fear of clusters of small holes. Rather than tone the scary images down, he fed them straight into Clive Barker’s Hellraiser: Revival.

The forthcoming first-person action-horror game drops players into a new story in Barker’s universe. Aidan Lynch must use the Genesis Configuration puzzle box to rescue his girlfriend from the Labyrinth as Pinhead, his Cenobites and a cult close in. But Revival is not built around jump scares. The team at Mad Head Games began with one question: what should players feel? The answer was discomfort.

“That’s a key emotion,” says Esov, “You know when you are looking at something, but you cannot look away?” Early in the game, players must push a hand inside a grotesque sculpture to retrieve an item – it’s all about feeling extreme unease. Even a stealth kill is drawn out rather than instant, he explains: “There is struggle. There is sweating, moaning. It’s really, really stressful.”

That does not mean simply filling every room with blood and bodies. Esov likens Pinhead to a monk rather than a traditional slasher villain: calm, imposing and “almost trolling you”. The horror comes from what he might do, but also the unnerving way he talks about doing it.

Clive Barker himself helped shape the characters, themes and rules of the universe, before staying on as an adviser as the story became a game. His feedback could move from big questions to one wonderfully specific request, which Esov recalls as: “Can you make the sky more purple in the Labyrinth?” Esov loved that “level of detailed nit-picking”, which showed that Barker was still watching over the world he created.

Doug Bradley also returns as Pinhead for the first time (except for a few lines in a time-limited chapter of Dead by Daylight) in the two decades since his last appearance in a Hellraiser film. Recording took place remotely, and Esov soon realised the actor needed little coaching. “You don’t have to direct him,” he says. “He actually is Pinhead!”

As for the Cenobites, they get more individual roles and screen time, but won’t be ordinary targets; their undeniable power had to survive the move into an action game. “You cannot fight them,” Esov says, “They’re not a gameplay aspect that you get to beat.”

Elsewhere, the first-person combat has drawn comparisons to Resident Evil and BioShock, while Condemned influenced the unpredictable melee fights. Around a quarter of the game takes place in the Labyrinth, and the Genesis Configuration works as both a key part of the story and a tool for the player. The difficulty settings include a highest level named after Hellraiser itself, which is how Esov prefers to play. His hellish serving suggestion of sorts: “It should be discomforting even to play.”

Esov hopes Revival will introduce a new audience to the mix of violence, sex, beauty and pain that sets Hellraiser apart. He wants a game “that doesn’t hold back”. If players come away disturbed, they will not be alone: Revival got under its own director’s skin before it ever had the chance to get under theirs.

GeneralTab.title: Middlesbrough murder investigation as two people die in fire
GeneralTab.text:
A murder investigation has been launched after two people died in a house fire.

The blaze in Grangetown, Middlesbrough, broke out just before 05:30 BST and also left a woman in hospital in a critical condition, alongside a further three people who suffered non-life threatening injuries.

Cleveland Police said it was investigating what had happened but was "keeping an open mind and cannot rule out any links to wider organised crime at this time".

The fire happened about two miles from the A66 crash that killed five young men and two police officers on Saturday morning.

Redcar and Cleveland Local Policing Commander Supt Emily Harrison said the force was working to "establish the circumstances of exactly what has happened".

"We will have a high visibility presence in the Grangetown area as this investigation progresses, and to provide reassurance to local communities, who will no doubt be impacted by this tragic incident."

Patrols have been increased in the local area to "reassure the local community", the force said.

GeneralTab.title: Prince Harry and Meghan land in UK
GeneralTab.text:
The Duke and Duchess of Sussex have arrived back in the UK, BBC News understands.

Prince Harry, Meghan and their children Archie and Lilibet are believed to have flown into the country privately from California.

A spokesman for the Duke and Duchess of Sussex said "this is not something we would comment on".

Last week, it was reported that the couple would be relocating to the UK in August. They will not return to official duties but will live in Britain as non-working royals.

It is thought the family will base themselves at a private property outside of London in the Cotswolds area.

Archie and Lilibet have been enrolled in school and the new term is due to start next week.

GeneralTab.title: Why high energy bills look like they are here to stay
GeneralTab.text:
Energy bills may have been a long way from our minds through the sweltering summer.

Clothes on a washing line have been drying in minutes. Cold showers have been more tempting than hot ones.

But the latest news and forecasts on gas prices will bring a renewed sense of worry and urgency to families, as well as government ministers.

Energy prices will rise by nearly 4% for millions of households in October. Even more striking is a prediction from the respected consultancy Cornwall Insight of a further 9% increase at the peak of winter in January.

With ongoing volatility in the wholesale gas market sparked by events in the Gulf region, the energy sector says high prices are here to stay.

EDF suggests bills will remain "stubbornly high" at their current level at least until the end of the decade.

High bills have, and continue to, bite. Energy prices have been central to the cost-of-living squeeze.

The typical household's dual-fuel bill is now 70% higher than it was at the start of 2021, before Russia's invasion of Ukraine.

That amounts to around £600 more each year than pre-crisis levels, according to industry body Energy UK.

Inevitably, more and more people have been unable to pay. Unpaid energy debt of more than three months is now at a record high, according to regulator Ofgem.

Suppliers, who chart debt levels for missed payments of a month or more, estimate total unpaid bills and charges to have reached £6bn. By the end of the year, they expect that to rise to £7bn.

The average household in debt, without a repayment plan, owes more than the typical annual bill.

And even if you are not in debt, you pay. Covering the cost of debt already adds about £60 to the average annual bill. Consultancy Baringa says everyone could, on average, be paying £100 to cover the cost of unpaid debts by the end of the year.

Someone who pays their bill on demand every three months, rather than a monthly direct debit, is typically already paying £150 a year to cover debt of others, owing to the greater risk of non-payment on this type of bill.

So, pressure on the government to help those most in need will only intensify.

Ofgem has a proposed debt relief scheme on the table, and campaigners keep telling them to get on with it, urging the government as to provide funding for it to be implemented.

Charities and the industry also want ministers to introduce a discounted tariff for those who need it most - based on benefits, health and income data.

Energy UK says a targeted plan would cost £1.9bn. That would be much cheaper than the £40bn commitment to protect everyone's bills after Russia invaded Ukraine.

But, who would pay? It could go on everyone else's bills. Or ministers could opt to raise taxes, borrow the money, or cancel spending elsewhere - all of which are tricky political choices.

Those who can have cut back on their energy use to reduce bills in recent years. Thermostats up and down the country have not been set as high as before. Batch cooking is more common.

So much so that Ofgem's official calculations for typical energy consumption were lowered again in July (to 9,500 kWh of gas and 2,500 kWh of electricity a year).

Millions have shifted onto fixed tariffs, with 35% of billpayers on such a deal.

So, many can justifiably say they have done their bit. Others who are older or who have health conditions might not have the luxury of lowering their energy use.

So, community warm hubs have become popular. Some became cold hubs during the hot summer so people could make use of the air con.

The heatwave has reduced the amount of energy stored across Europe, which needs to be restocked, piling more pressure on prices.

Add to that the huge cost of upgrading the UK's electricity network and you can see why there are predictions of longstanding high energy bills - irrespective of whether a lasting peace in the Iran war brings down the international price of wholesale gas.

GeneralTab.title: Reform proposes £30 tax rebate for HMRC phone delays
GeneralTab.text:
People on hold to HM Revenue and Customs (HMRC) for more than 30 minutes would get £30 off their tax bill under a Reform UK government, Robert Jenrick has announced.

Reform's economy spokesman said HMRC's treatment of taxpayers was "offensive to working people" and his party would tie the pay of senior HMRC officials to customer service targets.

To prevent abuse, the tax credit for phone delays would be limited to two occasions in a given tax year, Jenrick said.

HMRC has said it has improved its response times since a highly critical report by a committee of MPs, external, in January 2025, accused the organisation of seeking to "degrade its telephone service to drive taxpayers to digital channels".

The Public Accounts Committee report said nearly 44,000 customers were cut off without warning after being on hold for more than an hour in 2024 and "HMRC's treatment of taxpayers has damaged trust in the tax system".

Jenrick highlighted the findings - which were rejected as "completely baseless" by the then boss of HMRC - at a media conference in central London.

"Frankly, it is offensive to working people and I have had enough," said the former Tory MP.

"So, we will give HMRC a big incentive to actually provide proper customer service.

"I'm announcing today that under a Reform government, if you spend more than half an hour waiting for HMRC to answer your call, you will get a £30 credit off your tax bill. If HMRC delay, they can repay.

"And to make sure that the staff actually hit their targets, we'll tie the pay of senior HMRC officials to their customer service performance."

Jenrick also pledged to scrap UK privacy rules in favour of a "light-touch" approach to data protection as part of a bid to slash "red tape" for businesses.

He said the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR), which mirrors EU legislation and was adopted as domestic law after Brexit, had "strangled" tech firms and small enterprises.

The framework would be replaced by rules modelled on New Zealand's privacy legislation, which Reform says has the lightest-touch regime still recognised as being "adequate" by the EU.

Labour accused Reform of wanting to "scrap vital safeguards that protect people's private data" with its "unworkable and unserious plans".

HMRC has been contacted for a response.

articles.title: Middlesbrough murder investigation as two people die in fire
articles.text:
A murder investigation has been launched after two people died in a house fire.

The blaze in Grangetown, Middlesbrough, broke out just before 05:30 BST and also left a woman in hospital in a critical condition, alongside a further three people who suffered non-life threatening injuries.

Cleveland Police said it was investigating what had happened but was "keeping an open mind and cannot rule out any links to wider organised crime at this time".

The fire happened about two miles from the A66 crash that killed five young men and two police officers on Saturday morning.

Redcar and Cleveland Local Policing Commander Supt Emily Harrison said the force was working to "establish the circumstances of exactly what has happened".

"We will have a high visibility presence in the Grangetown area as this investigation progresses, and to provide reassurance to local communities, who will no doubt be impacted by this tragic incident."

Patrols have been increased in the local area to "reassure the local community", the force said.

articles.title: Ex-chief constable being investigated by IOPC over Israeli fan ban
articles.text:
The former chief constable of West Midlands Police is being investigated by the police watchdog for gross misconduct over the banning of Israeli Maccabi Tel Aviv fans from a match against Aston Villa.

The Independent Office for Police Conduct (IOPC) has given notice that it is investigating Craig Guildford, as well as three police officers and a staff member.

The IOPC launched an independent investigation in January to examine the involvement of West Midlands Police officers in the planning and preparation of the match at Villa Park on 6 November 2025.

The ban attracted national and international debate, with the government saying it would do everything in its power to have it overturned.

The IOPC said evidence indicated that Guildford "may have had oversight on an intelligence briefing document presented to the safety advisory group (SAG) that was later reported to have contained inaccuracies and misleading information".

It is alleged the briefing document "gave an imbalanced view of the risk away fans posed", contributing to the decision to ban the supporters.

The police watchdog added: "We consider Mr Guildford may have failed to ensure due diligence and the highest level of scrutiny over such an influential document."

A senior serving officer, who played a lead role in compiling the briefing, is under investigation for allegedly failing to ensure its accuracy.

The watchdog said the officer may not have accurately represented some information which could have resulted in the briefing "lacking impartiality".

They are also examining whether the officer "may have failed to appropriately handle sensitive intelligence" contained in the report, before it was shared with SAG members.

The staff member, who was involved in researching and compiling intelligence for the game, is alleged to have sourced inaccurate information from AI searches and took no subsequent action to help ensure it was not included in briefings.

Two other senior serving officers who played important roles in the force's planning for the game have been notified they are being investigated for potential misconduct.

It is alleged one was not sufficiently diligent in the exercise of their duties in overseeing the operation, including balancing operational needs alongside engaging with local Jewish communities, and that they displayed a lack of impartiality towards Maccabi fans in both external and internal communications.

The other officer will be investigated in relation to their oversight of the briefing document and an allegation that they too lacked balance in references to Maccabi supporters.

A dedicated investigation team at the IOPC has examined more than 600 pieces of evidence, including operational documents, reports, intelligence research, minutes of meetings, and a large volume of correspondence including emails and messages.

The IOPC's director of engagement, Derrick Campbell, said: "Our investigation to date has been to assess whether there is an indication anyone may have breached one or more of the standards of police professional behaviour.

"We have examined a wealth of material, hundreds of pieces of evidence, and believe there is an indication some people serving with the police may potentially have behaved in a manner that could justify disciplinary proceedings.

"They have been informed their conduct will be investigated. At the end of our investigation, we will decide if anyone has a case to answer and should face a misconduct meeting or hearing."

Campbell added that the serving of notices did not necessarily mean that disciplinary proceedings would follow, saying all decisions would be kept under review as the investigation progressed.

West Midlands Police's temporary deputy chief constable, Jen Mattinson, said that she undertook a voluntary referral to the IOPC on her first full day in the role regarding conduct matters by senior officers and staff.

"This referral was made prior to the IOPC announcement to use their 'power of initiative' to independently investigate if any officer or staff member may have a case to answer for misconduct," Mattinson said.

"We recognise that the public's trust in West Midlands Police has been damaged by this event and we have worked hard over the last seven months - and continue to do so - to rebuild confidence in the force.

"We will continue to fully engage and cooperate with the IOPC as their work continues."

articles.title: Household energy bills to hit three-year high as Ofgem announces 4% rise from October
articles.text:
Energy prices for millions of households will rise to the highest level for three years, under regulator Ofgem's price cap.

Ofgem said the price cap will increase by 4% on 1 October, driven by higher wholesale gas prices due to the Iran war.

A household using a typical amount of gas and electricity will pay £60 a year more, but more than a third of households are on fixed tariffs so their prices will not change.

The government said its cut to VAT on electricity bills will save households £45 and it was doing more to address cost of living pressures, but opposition parties said Labour was not doing enough.

The new cap will hit household bills as the colder weather arrives in October.

Suppliers say energy debt has rocketed and, with high bills likely to persist, have called for more support for those struggling to pay.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham acknowledged people would find the increase "difficult" but highlighted his move to cut VAT from electricity bills, which he said would help from October.

He said the government would "continue to look... at how we get energy prices down in the long term".

As well as the VAT cut, the government said the warm homes discount would take £150 off bills for six million households this winter.

But analysts at the energy consultancy Cornwall Insight have forecast domestic energy prices may rise a further 9% in the new year, bringing renewed concern to households during the coldest months.

Shadow energy secretary Claire Coutinho said the government must "put cheap energy first", saying while it had promised to cut bills by £300 they had "gone up by nearly £400 instead".

Liberal Democrat spokesperson for energy and net zero Pippa Heylings said Burnham needed to "wake up to the scale of the challenge" and make bold changes to lower bills.

Reform UK treasury spokesperson Robert Jenrick said households faced a "difficult period ahead" and said Labour's "net zero ideology" is driving up bills.

Former Prime Minister Gordon Brown also weighed in, saying the government should introduce a "machine gaming tax" and use proceeds to help those struggling with bills.

Longer term, he said Burnham should look at a social tariff for energy.

"I think Andy Burnham, I know him well, will want to do something along the lines I'm suggesting," he said.

Neil Kenward, Ofgem's director general for markets, said while gas bills were rising by 8%, electricity bills were actually falling slightly due to the government's VAT cut.

He said the gap between gas and electricity bills meant it would be cheaper for households to transition to heat pumps.

Around 35% of households - or 11 million households - are on fixed tariffs, but 22 million in England, Wales and Scotland are on tariffs affected by the price cap.

Ofgem said the price cap will rise by £60 per year – or £5 per month – to £1,723 for the typical household using both electricity and gas and paying by direct debit if this level was sustained for a year.

Kenward told the Today programme the rise was technically 3.6%, but Ofgem always rounds the number which is why it publicised the 4% figure.

Kenward added: "Savings are available by choosing a fixed tariff, which are available at £100 or more below the October price cap."

The energy cap sets a maximum price for each unit of gas and electricity, not the total bill, so a household's final bill depends on their usage.

In July, Ofgem reduced what it believes to be a "typical" level of energy use, because many homes have cut back owing to high prices of recent years while energy efficiency has improved.

Its new estimate is 9,500 kWh of gas and 2,500 kWh of electricity a year.

Vanessa Northam, director at debt charity StepChange, said the increasing number of people seeking help often had high energy debt, averaging at £2,600 on top of other financial commitments.

The charity has joined calls for the government to introduce a social tariff.

Her advice for those who might only just be managing as winter approaches includes:

Taking stock of all household money coming in and going out

Look closely at how much energy you are using, and be alert if there are a series of estimated bills, which might prove to be inaccurate

Telling your supplier if you think you are going to struggle

Some information is available online, but it is often best to try to talk to someone who can fully understand your situation

Suppliers offer various support schemes to anyone struggling to pay, or who is likely to find it difficult.

Energy UK has a list of these schemes, external. But it stresses companies can often only help if you tell your supplier you are unable to pay.

articles.title: Islamabad PIMS hospital fire: Witnesses say rescue was delayed as blaze killed 14 babies
articles.text:
It was just after dawn on Wednesday morning at a maternity ward in the Pakistani capital when a horrific blaze erupted.

It would go on to kill 14 infants as parents say they waited hours for help to arrive.

Hivsa Walid was near the room at the Pakistan Institute of Medical Sciences (PIMS) hospital with her sister-in-law, who had given birth days earlier. She initially heard a shout and thought a patient had died - but then she saw smoke.

The pair fled with the baby, who is so small she does not yet have a name.

"We didn't even think about our belongings. We just grabbed the baby and rushed downstairs.

"Some patients had delivered their babies just that night. I don't even know how we managed to get down - it was all a blur."

The fire broke out in an air-conditioning unit on the third floor of the mother and child unit at PIMS, one of the main state-run hospitals in Islamabad. Only one of the 15 babies present was saved.

Khurram Mehmood, 40, told AFP news agency there was a long wait for rescue workers. "I lost my daughter. She was only three days old," he said.

Jaweria, the mother of another victim, told AFP news agency the door to the maternity ward was locked.

"For two hours I kept crying and wailing," she said. "Police arrived after four hours and said they are here to investigate."

"Why did the doctors leave the children there?" she asks.

"To hell with you, rescue team and police. Babies burnt to death there, but nobody could save them."

Rana Imran Sikander, the hospital's executive director, told the BBC the ward's door was not locked but was manned. He cited the need to protect babies from being stolen, something that has happened before at government hospitals.

Walid suggested PIMS's safety protocols were inadequate, despite it being a major hospital. "There should have been fire extinguishers and protocols, but no one was doing anything - everyone was just running."

The father of a baby who died told Reuters he had been visiting the ward for eight days and the building had "no fire security, no proper exits".

"All doors were closed, only one door was for us to visit our children. They kept the other doors locked because they feared we would come to see our children too often."

Several eyewitnesses have claimed duty staff were not around.

People had to "break the door down" and rescue teams were forced to smash the windows to control the flames, a witness who did not give her name told AFP.

Abdul Ghafoor, another witness, told AFP he tried to get into the building to rescue patients but couldn't reach the maternity ward.

"There was thick black smoke inside and patients were trapped," he said. "Rescue teams arrived after almost two hours."

articles.title: CIA chief held talks with Russian intelligence services, Kremlin says
articles.text:
The head of the US Central Intelligence Agency (CIA) John Ratcliffe has met Russia's intelligence services during his visit to Moscow, the Kremlin has said.

Ratcliffe travelled to the Russian capital on Tuesday in a rare and unannounced visit.

"There were contacts with the intelligence services," Vladimir Putin's press secretary, Dmitry Peskov, told reporters.

"There were no meetings with the president of Russia. That's all I can say on the subject. Naturally, President Putin is briefed immediately about everything," he added.

Peskov made the comments in response to a question at his daily press briefing from a reporter at the Russian newspaper Rossiyskaya Gazeta, who asked if Vladimir Putin was informed about the CIA chief meetings and "at what level" they were held.

Putin's spokesman was also asked by the BBC's Russia Editor Steve Rosenberg what was the topic of the CIA talks.

"I have nothing to add to what I've already said on the subject," Peskov replied.

It was too early to say what impact this meeting would have over repairing bilateral US Russian relations, he said.

"How much this will impact the overall process of recovering our bilateral relations from the profound crisis they're currently in, it is premature to say."

But contacts between intelligence agencies are "a positive phenomenon, a positive process," Peskov added, saying they often continue "even during the most difficult moments" in relations between the two countries.

Ratcliffe appears to be one of the highest-ranking US officials to visit Russia during President Donald Trump's second term.

In-person talks between high-level American and Russian officials are rare.

The last time a CIA director visited Moscow was in November 2021 - when William Burns warned Russia against sending troops into Ukraine. Weeks later, the Kremlin launched its full-scale war on Ukraine.

Since then, the US has had strained relations with Russia, which has been isolated on the world stage and faced international economic sanctions.

Trump met Russian President Vladimir Putin at a summit in Alaska last year but the meeting did not lead to a breakthrough. Subsequent US-led peace talks between Russia and Ukraine appear to have stalled.

Ahead of the trip, the US told Ukraine that a senior delegation would be travelling to Moscow and asked Kyiv to suspend strikes until they had left, a senior Ukrainian official told CBS.

John Foreman, who served as a British military attaché to Moscow between 2019 and 2022, told Radio 4's PM programme: "The Americans don't normally send such a high ranking official to Moscow unannounced at short notice unless something is up."

BBC News has contacted the CIA, the White House and Pentagon for comment.

articles.title: How Dolly Parton helped the world - from children's books to supporting Covid vaccine
articles.text:
Dolly Parton will not only be remembered for her iconic songs and Southern charm, but also for her philanthropic work.

Throughout her life, she supported communities in need, especially in her home state of Tennessee. She funded medical research that led to one of the first Covid-19 vaccines, donated to wildfire victims and even helped the once-endangered bald eagle, America's national bird.

But it is her Imagination Library - the mainstay of her charity work - that has helped millions of children learn to read by sending out free books.

The programme was inspired by her father who couldn't read or write.

"I think deep down inside, my daddy was prouder of [the library] than he even was of my career," she wrote.

Parton established her non-profit organisation, the Dollywood Foundation, in 1988, to help bolster children's education. Its efforts are practical - like sending out books - and often goes directly to the grass roots, where it can really make a difference, fast.

In the early 90s, Parton said she'd give every seventh and eighth-grade student (ages 12 to 14) in Sevier County, Tennessee, where she grew up, $500 if they graduated high school. They had to have a buddy, to keep each other in check - which in turn made more children graduate.

Sure, it was a bit of a bribe, but it worked - the drop out rate went from 35% to 6%, according to the foundation's website.

"I'm kind of addicted to the feeling of giving," she once said. "Knowing that I'm doing something good for someone else."

Parton was awarded the Carnegie Medal of Philanthropy in 2022, which honoured her as "one of the entertainment world's most generous philanthropists".

Dolly Parton was one of 12 children born into a poor family that lived in a one-bedroom cabin in the Smoky Mountains. Her hardworking father, Robert Lee Parton, was a tobacco farmer.

"He was the smartest man I have ever known but I know in my heart his inability to read probably kept him from fulfilling all of his dreams," Dolly wrote.

Inspired by this, the Imagination Library was launched in 1995, with the help of Robert Parton. It sends out free books to children younger than five every month.

The programme was originally set up just for those in Sevier County - but it quickly went national and then global. The Imagination Library now sends books to children across the US, Canada, UK, Ireland and Australia.

According to its website, more than 332.4 million books have been sent out.

For many children who have never owned their own book, it is a special gift just for them.

"It's the fact they get recognised," Parton once said. "They get this little book with their little name on it in the mail, and they feel special... they know that somebody out there is thinking of them."

"That vision she had about books and this understanding of sharing stories was remarkable," Eileen Driver, the chair of the Stokesley Imagination Library in the UK, told the BBC's Radio Tees.

Scottish National Party councillor, Lee Mills - admittedly a superfan from a young age - said when he was elected he set out to bring the Imagination Library to Dundee.

"Dolly's legacy will last with every page turned of a children's book. I will do my utmost best to ensure that this is delivered to every child in Scotland," he told the BBC.

British author Selina Brown, whose book My Rice is Best was one of those selected to be distributed, told the BBC it was quite emotional to see 14,000 copies of her book being packed up, ready to post.

"For my book in particular, the protagonist is black. It helps with representation, it helps with real life situations and having a book that speaks directly to you and speaks to a different world is important."

During Covid, Parton started reading some of the books aloud, in recordings on YouTube for children - many of whom didn't know who she was.

"You mean she sings, too?" exclaimed one boy when he found out, Linda Jinnette Cooper wrote on the library's Facebook page.

In 2020, as the Covid-19 pandemic gripped the world, Parton encouraged people to get vaccinated and donated $1m (£716,000) to the Vanderbilt University Medical Center in Nashville, which helped fund the Moderna vaccine.

A portion of the money went towards funding an early stage-trial of the Moderna vaccine, which found it to offer nearly 95% protection against severe Covid-19.

Reimagining her hit song, Jolene, Parton changed the lyrics to "vaccine, vaccine, vaccine, vaccine, I'm begging of you, please don't hesitate".

She showed herself being injected, saying: "I'm old enough to get it and I'm smart enough to get it."

Parton donated to medical research several times over the years.

A benefit concert in 2007 raised $1m for a new hospital and cancer centre in Sevier County, which includes a Dolly Parton Center for Women's Services.

Ten years later, she released a children's album, I Believe in You, and donated another $1m, this time to Nashville's Monroe Carell Jr. Children's Hospital at Vanderbilt University Medical Center, after her niece was treated for leukaemia there.

She donated yet another $1m to the hospital a few years later, this time to help paediatric infectious disease research.

"I love children," Parton said in a statement at the time. "No child should ever have to suffer, and I'm willing to do my part to try and keep as many of them as I can as healthy and safe as possible."

And earlier this year, the East Tennessee Children's Hospital announced it would be renamed to the Dolly Parton Children's Hospital, after the star partnered with the not-for-profit facility.

Her Dollywood amusement park has a lot more than rollercoasters - it's also home to the largest sanctuary for non-releasable bald eagles in the world.

Managed by the American Eagle Foundation, its rehabilitation and breeding work has won awards and in 2007, the bald eagle was removed from the endangered species list.

In 2022, Parton's charity work to improve education was extended to adults, when it was announced that any Dollywood employee - whether they were seasonal, part-time or full-time, would have 100% of their tuition and books paid for if they furthered their education.

In announcing her death on Tuesday, Parton's team asked fans to donate to the Imagination Library, instead of sending flowers, so that her legacy can continue for many years to come.

"When I'm done, I can rest in peace knowing I've done my best," Parton once said.

"I hope that when my time comes, I'll leave something behind that others can use to lift themselves up."

Additional reporting by Olivia Ireland

articles.title: Why Tesla has been caught up in a massive car recall in China
articles.text:
Hidden car door handles - the sleek designs often found on electric vehicles (EVs) - have come under the spotlight over the past week.

That's after China announced its biggest ever recall of cars, with more than four million vehicles - mostly Teslas - affected.

The recall comes ahead of new regulations in China, requiring cars to have a mechanical release both on the inside and outside of their doors.

Popularised by Elon Musk's electric vehicle giant, this type of handle has become commonplace around the world.

But several incidents have raised concerns that this design may make doors difficult to open in an emergency.

Hidden door handles are widely used in modern cars in China, with around 60% of the top 100 best-selling new energy vehicles, including EVs and hybrids, having them.

The minimalist design gives vehicles a "sleek look and reduces wind drag" but can be confusing to use, car industry analyst Stephen Dyer from consultancy AlixPartners told the BBC.

"Even I often find it difficult to locate the switch to open the door from the inside of an unfamiliar vehicle," said Dyer, who is based in Shanghai.

But beyond their usability, the handles have been blamed for endangering the lives of drivers and passengers.

Electronically powered door handles became an industry trend, but raised "real safety concerns" when doors failed to open promptly, delaying rescue efforts after accidents, said Nanyang Technological University associate professor Lyu Chen.

"A door handle may seem simple, but it becomes safety-critical in the seconds after a crash," Chen said.

Chinese carmaker Xiaomi faced intense scrutiny following two fatal crashes in 2025 involving its SU7 model, when suspected electrical failures allegedly trapped occupants.

One of the incidents took place on a highway in Tongling city, eastern China, killing three people, according to regional news coverage cited by state-controlled media Global Times.

Relatives of the victims said the passengers were stuck in the car as the vehicle's doors could not be unlocked after the collision, the outlet said.

At the time, Xiaomi's representatives said the SU7 had mechanical emergency release handles that function even without power, which are located at the bottom of each door.

The company added at the time that it was investigating the matter and cooperating with the police.

The latest models of the SU7 come with new door handles that can be opened without power.

Xiaomi has not responded to BBC requests for comment.

Tesla has also faced lawsuits in the US over its door handle designs.

The company has been sued by the only survivor of a crash in 2024 involving a Cybertruck - Tesla's electric pickup - that killed three college students in California.

Survivor Jordan Miller alleged that the Cybertruck's design trapped passengers in the burning vehicle and blocked their rescue.

The car did not have door handles and the electronic buttons meant to open the doors failed to work, according to his lawyers from The Veen Firm.

"When you design a vehicle with no mechanical way to open the doors from the outside, you are betting the electronics will work in every scenario, including a high-speed crash followed by a fire," said one of the lawyers in a statement.

In court filings, Tesla denied any wrongdoing and said the Cybertruck is compliant with US federal safety standards, the Guardian reported.

There have been other cases in the US of passengers, including children, allegedly being trapped in Tesla cars after the doors suddenly stopped working.

The BBC has contacted Tesla for comment.

In February, China said it would ban hidden door handles, making it the first country to do so.

The new rules, which take effect on 1 January 2027, mean new car designs without physical release mechanisms on the inside and outside of their doors cannot be sold.

The cars' interior must also carry signs to show how to open the door.

The measures in China come ahead of the US and European Union, which typically lead regulations around road safety and emissions, Dyer noted.

One reason is likely to be the sheer number of EVs in China, he added.

On 21 August, China's State Administration for Market Regulation (SAMR) announced that Tesla and some major Chinese car makers - including Xiaomi, XPeng and Geely - would recall more than four million vehicles.

The manufacturers were ordered to add warning labels inside vehicle doors to show passengers how to open them. Some cars will also get a software update that will lower their windows in the event of a crash.

Tesla, which started selling the Model S sedan with hidden door handles in China in 2014, is recalling nearly three million cars, according to the SAMR.

The agency said the recalled cars have door handles that are "difficult to identify" because they are a similar colour to the vehicle's interior trim.

In the event of an electrical failure, the handles' design may also prevent passengers from quickly opening the doors to escape or "hinder rescue efforts" by bystanders, the SAMR added.

Xiaomi, XPeng and Geely will also recall a total of more than 750,000 vehicles.

The US National Highway Traffic Safety Administration told the BBC that it is reviewing whether it will require emergency door-exit systems in vehicles.

In Europe, regulators have flagged the potential hazards related to hidden handles and drafted new standards to ensure they still work even if a car's power is cut off.

Engineering lecturer Lyu Chen said that while concealed door handles are still common in EV designs, manufacturers and regulators are paying increasing attention to how they design their doors.

Since cars are built to sell globally, it is likely that the safety requirements in China will be adopted elsewhere, he added.

"The common principle is clear: emergency entry and exit should remain possible even after a loss of electrical power."

articles.title: Canada announces 'dollar-for-dollar' retaliatory tariffs on US as high as 50%
articles.text:
Canada has announced counter-tariffs as high as 50% on a range of US goods in retaliation to the latest wave of levies on Canadian imports imposed by President Donald Trump last weekend.

The Canadian tariffs will apply to nearly C$28bn ($20bn; £15bn) worth of American products, ranging from steel to furniture, fresh tuna and cotton T-shirts, officials announced on Tuesday.

The list of targeted products is designed to match Canadian goods hit by the US. The Canadian levies are set to come into effect on 8 September.

It is the latest escalation after US-Canada trade talks collapsed late last week, with each side accusing the other of making last-minute demands that were unreasonable.

Finance Minister François-Philippe Champagne said that Canada's retaliation is in response to 50% tariffs imposed by the Trump administration on a range of Canadian goods after trade talks fell apart on Friday.

"Those tariffs will have real consequences for Canadian workers, businesses and communities across our nation," he said. "Canada must respond."

Champagne characterised Canada's retaliation as "proportionate" and "strategic".

He added that Canada will also offer businesses and workers impacted by US tariffs an additional C$7.5bn for support programmes designed to minimise job losses and keep companies afloat.

Placing taxes on trade between what are historically two of the world's closest trading partners will undoubtedly lead to pain on both sides of the border.

Supply chains which have been developed over decades are set to see increased trading costs due the latest tariff announcements made from both the US and Canada, ultimately hitting businesses of all sizes and consumers through potentially higher prices.

Polls suggest the majority of Canadians support their government in holding firm against the US.

But some questions remain on exactly why trade talks fell apart, with the Conservative opposition asking that the full text of the draft deal with the US be released.

Businesses have also expressed concerns about the impact of a prolonged trade war with Canada's largest trading partner.
